column17: Other: Seeking to attract buyers.
column19:
The City of Atlanta launched its urban forest carbon credit program in 2022 with the Lake Charlotte Nature Preserve Carbon Credit Project. This initiative preserves 196 acres of ecologically high value forest and has issued 36,265 Carbon Plus credits through a 40 year urban tree preservation protocol. The program is designed to generate revenue over more than four decades that supports preservation and stewardship, delivering co benefits in public health, air quality, stormwater management, and energy savings. Currently 27,717 credits are available for purchase, with credits issued annually at approximately 9,239 per year for 2023, 2024, and 2025.

Building on this success, the City is now expanding the program to include four newly acquired forested nature preserve properties: Southwest Nature Preserve, Utoy Creek Nature Preserve, Mount Zion Nature Preserve, and South River Nature Preserve, totaling approximately 252 acres. These areas were acquired between late 2022 and 2023 through deed, park impact fees, and tree trust funds.

This expansion continues the strategy of leveraging carbon credit revenue to preserve mature urban canopies from development pressures, bolster climate resilience, and fund ecosystem stewardship. It aligns with broader City goals of enhancing equitable greenspace access within walking distance for all residents, advancing greenhouse gas reduction efforts, and strengthening resilience through nature based strategies. Importantly, this carbon credit model is structured to continue scaling across all future forested property acquisitions the City makes, encouraging ongoing preservation while also generating additional revenue that can be reinvested to compound environmental and community impact over time.

The City is actively seeking partners to purchase these premium Carbon Plus credits and help spread the word about their availability. By connecting with buyers who value high quality, community centered offsets, the City can accelerate reinvestment in further preservation and resilience projects. At the same time, Atlanta hopes that showcasing this model will inspire other local governments to launch similar initiatives, demonstrating how urban forest preservation can serve as both a climate mitigation tool and a revenue generating pathway to fund long term adaptation.

Project documentation and credits available for purchase can be found here. Lake Charlotte Nature Preserve Carbon Credit Project Page : https://www.cityforestcredits.org/carbon-credits/carbon-registry/atlanta-forest-carbon-offsets/

City of Atlanta's Carbon Credit Program Expansion: https://www.cityforestcredits.org/carbon-credits/carbon-registry/city-of-atlanta-carbon-credit-program-2024/

As the City works to transition its fleet to zero emission and low emission vehicles, especially EV's, and lead, partner and support the installation of 250 new EV charging ports through 2025 as well as aligning with Climate Mayor's 500% increase in EV charging by 2030. 

Atlanta Fire Foundation's fleet forward campaign has purchased the first two EV emergency response vehicles (Rivian R1T's) for our Atlanta Fire Rescue Department's Fleet but is still raising in its $3 million capital goal to purchase the City first EV Fire Truck (Rosenbauer) 

CFI Grant: $11.8M (USDOT/FHWA CFI, announced Aug 27, 2024). Scope is a 50-port DC fast-charging hub at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport to serve rental fleets, rideshare, hotel shuttles, airport employees, City fleet (light-heavy duty), and the traveling public on adjacent interstates. Status: In early 2025, federal EV-charging funds were paused/frozen. Atlanta's CFI award remains treated as “frozen” pending clear federal direction on Georgia resumption, so the City is maintaining project readiness while the pause is resolved.

3rd Party owned charging on City owned property model: A cost-neutral (potentially revenue-generating) partnership in which a private EV charging provider owns, finances, installs, operates, and maintains DCFC and L2 chargers on City sites and eligible right-of-way; the City grants site access/licenses and receives revenue share or site-host fees. This approach is consistent with established right-of-way licensing and public-private EVSE best practices used by peer cities. This is currently in the process of the City's procurement Department to move forward. 

CHDV Grant: The City of Atlanta was awarded $3.2 million through the EPA's Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicles (CHDV) program to accelerate the electrification of its municipal fleet. Under this grant, the City will deploy seven medium- and heavy-duty zero-emission vehicles (including refuse and utility trucks, a street sweeper, and transit-style shuttles) and seven 150-kW DC fast chargers across four priority municipal sites. An earlier proposal to electrify four Department of Aviation buses was deemed ineligible, reducing the total scope to seven vehicles and seven chargers. The project, known as EcoFleet ATL, will deliver measurable reductions in greenhouse gas and criteria pollutant emissions, improve air quality in overburdened neighborhoods, and build workforce capacity through mechanic and operator EV training. It also represents the City's first dedicated heavy-duty EV and DC fast charging deployments, serving as a foundation for scaling electrification across Atlanta's municipal fleet. However, rising tariff prices on both EVs and charging infrastructure have significantly increased project costs, making external funding (like Georgia Power's Make Ready Program) important to closing budget gaps and maximizing successful implementation.

The City of Atlanta formally adopted the Trails ATL master plan on June 16, 2025, through unanimous City Council approval, integrating it into the City's Comprehensive Development Plan and establishing the policy framework needed to move into implementation. As part of this bold 30 year vision, the plan targets a total network of 535 miles of multi use trails designed to connect neighborhoods, parks, schools, transit corridors, and greenways, ultimately enabling 95 percent of residents to access an 'all ages, all abilities' trail within a 10 minute walk or wheelchair ride by 2052.

Phase I of Trails ATL is scoped to deliver approximately 35 miles of new greenways and protected street trails spanning neighborhoods like Lakewood Heights, South Atlanta, Buckhead, and southwest Atlanta over a buildout decade from 2027 to 2037. This first phase carries an estimated price tag of $252 million, reflecting December 2024 labor and materials pricing, with some trails to include lighting but excluding costs for security cameras, real estate acquisition, easements, etc.

To date, while more than 100 miles of trails have already been completed or are currently funded through existing infrastructure, the Trails ATL plan remains reliant on securing dedicated funding. Proposed sources include local bonds or levies such as a Transportation Special Local Option Sales Tax (TSPLOST) anticipated for 2027, alongside state and federal grants, philanthropic contributions, and partnerships. These funding pathways are essential to launch Phase I and sustain the ongoing project conveyor belt strategy, ensuring design, permitting, and construction phases are continuously active.

column19: We propose to work in two phases: first, to build a complete, robust inventory of refrigerant and refrigerant-bearing equipment within the portfolio of buildings the City owns or controls. The results of the inventory will be used to calculate the scope of Austin's emissions risk posed by these gases. This phase is currently in progress, and a consultant has been retained to support its completion. Second, we will use this inventory analysis and inputs drawn from direct engagement with Austin stakeholders to develop a strategy for efficiently and responsibly managing those refrigerants. This strategy will focus on accelerating the transition from high Global Warming Potential (GWP) cooling systems to low GWP alternatives. Where available, we will provide immediate end-of-life solutions for decommissioning systems, with particular priority placed on those that still utilize particularly potent and high impact refrigerants like chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs).Lessons learned from the city's inventorying of refrigerants and strategies for managing these refrigerants will inform future incentive or regulatory programs to manage refrigerants in buildings the city does not own or control.

column19: The Barcelona Sustainable Energy Mechanism (MES Barcelona), a tool to support and accelerate the city's energy transition alongside private investors. The tool is intended to encourage investment in solar panelling and energy renewal in the city.The mechanism's priority aim is to boost the production of photovoltaic energy in the city based on private initiatives, focusing on projects that use both large spaces (the roofs of industrial buildings and warehouses, of office buildings or of other places in the city) and roofs and flat rooftops of residential buildings by grouping together several residential buildings which, together, can make the entire investment manageable as well as scalable. In addition, investments are expected to be made in energy renovation projects for buildings with a high energy consumption, such as hospitals, hotels and sports facilities. Finally, MES Barcelona also intends to invest in projects to boost innovation in the renewable energy economic sector.MES Barcelona is a financial investment mechanism from Barcelona City Council. This €50-million municipal endowment will therefore be used for investment projects proposed by City Council-approved investors. These approved investors are a group of investors with experience investing in photovoltaic installations and energy renovation. When it comes to selecting investments, the City Council will require these to focus on either photovoltaic solar panel installations or energy renovation where the business model does not require co-funding from the owners of the buildings. Investors will contribute 100% of the investment, which they will recover through the surplus energy or energy savings resulting from the operations funded by them. In the case of investors specialising in photovoltaic energy, among other criteria, there will be a guarantee that these funds diversify the installation of photovoltaic solar panels in several types of building (residential, tertiary and industrial buildings) and encourage self-consumption, energy communities and the installation of electric vehicle charging points and so on. Private investors will be able to suggest improvements regarding the use and exploitation of community roofs.In March 2021, Barcelona City Council's Economy and Tax Office Commission approved the first companies and business groups that can be approved investors in the Barcelona Sustainable Energy Mechanism (MESBarcelona). These companies are: Endesa; GVC; Accelera Energia; Iberdrola; Naturgy Iberia, SA; Suma Capital SGECR, SA; Hengdian Group / ENERparking Sunstroom, i Intermoney Titulización SGFT, SA. The diversity of companies enables very diversified investment strategies to be proposed, encompassing different types of buildings and actions: residential buildings, offices, industrial warehouses, car parks, and public infrastructures and buildings committed to implementing clean energy (solar panels), building renovation, and even the possible production of green hydrogen. The investor approval process is open-ended, so start-ups will be able to join the MESBarcelona project in upcoming calls. Initially, there will be two calls per year, in addition to the new approval calls that will emerge.

In November 2022, the City of Chicago announced a pilot project to divert household food scraps into composting through six community garden sites. The project was implemented in collaboration with the nonprofit NeighborSpace and was partially funded through the National Resources Defense Council. The announcement embedded the project in the city's effort to explore waste reuse strategies that contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Six gardens were chosen across Chicago in collaboration with the nonprofit NeighborSpace. 

All six gardens composted food scraps during 2023; gardens acted as environmental education
sites, introducing participants to the practice and importance of composting.
100+ food scrap participants participated in the program across six community gardens and
the majority of participants lived in proximity to their submission garden. Gardens established unique systems for collecting food scraps in ways that were culturally relevant to their community. 

Chicago has great potential to divert food scrap waste from landfills. A 2021 study of Chicago
waste generation estimated 522,510 tons of organic waste annually, almost half of which
originates in single-family households. The study recommends investment in residential
source reduction and community education programs. Evaluation data demonstrates that the
program addressed both recommendations (Delta Institute, 2021).

The transportation sector is the second highest source of GHG emissions in Chicago and is a major contributor to poor air quality in our region. CDOT and the City more broadly are focused on lowering emissions from the transportation sector while improving air quality, increasing residents' mobility and job access, lowering household transportation costs, and improving public health.
The Charge Up Chicago! Chicago Community Resources and Charging Infrastructure Implementation (CUC) project will bring unique community benefits to Chicago by enabling equitable access to electric vehicles and E-mobility options in the city. CUC will then invest in community developed and owned charging station projects in addition to City of Chicago owned public charging stations. Leveraging the geographic diversity and equitable access mission of the Chicago Public Libraries, City-owned stations will be deployed at libraries to fill gaps in existing charging infrastructure, support high density multifamily housing communities, and create shared-use charging access to expand the City's EV municipal fleet in addition to ride hail, taxi and rental EV fleets serving Midway Airport. 

Currently, there are 720 publicly available EV passenger vehicle chargers in Chicago. Every community has registered EVs, but 70% of all public charging stations are concentrated in just three Community Areas. Of the 77 total Community Areas in Chicago, 47 do not have any public charging stations. The South and West Sides of Chicago have few public locations for Level 2 charging and virtually no access to DC fast charging.

Under this program, which is commonly found in other parts of the country, owners of existing commercial properties will be able to finance up to 100 percent of the cost of energy efficiency improvements and renewable energy projects for up to 25 years through a special assessment placed on the property. New Orleans faces an existential stormwater management crisis due to its low-lying geography, aging infrastructure, and the increasing impacts of climate change, including intense rainfall and rising sea levels. The city's flood risk is driven by a complex mix of factors—outdated drainage systems, urban development, subsidence, and inadequate resources for drainage maintenance or upgrades—making it difficult to understand and prioritize solutions. The challenge is compounded by the need for a systematic approach to evaluate and fund diverse stormwater projects amid competing needs and limited budgets. 

This project proposes the development of a Stormwater Master Plan that will create a data-driven, systematic framework to identify, evaluate, and prioritize stormwater management projects. After reviewing and aligning existing capital investments with relevant strategic plans and previous studies, this plan will integrate both traditional drainage improvements and green infrastructure solutions while leveraging advanced modeling to guide decision-making. A core component of this effort is robust community engagement, ensuring that residents, particularly those in vulnerable neighborhoods, have a voice in shaping the plan's priorities and solutions. 

Our intended outcomes include reduced flood risks, enhanced public safety, and improved environmental quality, focusing on equity and sustainability. By involving the community in the planning process, we aim to ensure that the plan reflects local needs and values, fostering trust and ownership among residents.

The City of New Orleans plans to increase recycling rates and landfill diversion, and seeks to evaluate its waste and recycling infrastructure options to support development of a state-of-the-art materials recovery facility (MRF) and an associated recycling markets hub for small businesses. In fall 2023, the City received a $3.98 million Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling (SWIFR) grant, which includes funding for curbside cart expansion, education and outreach, and the creation of a 10-year Solid Waste Master Plan to guide future diversion efforts.

However, the lack of regional processing capacity poses a direct threat to the long-term success of this grant. While the SWIFR award is designed to expand access to recycling and strengthen diversion programs, the city's existing MRF is already strained. Without sufficient processing infrastructure, the expanded residential collection program risks overwhelming the system, undercutting the community benefits envisioned by the grant.

Local media has highlighted the stakes: the City's recycling expansion effort, expected to bring service to more than 70,000 additional households, cannot be fully realized unless New Orleans develops or partners for modern processing infrastructure. Estimates for building a state-of-the-art MRF and recycling hub range from $15-20 million, a scale of investment that will be necessary to ensure the SWIFR program's momentum translates into durable and resilient waste diversion.

The strategy sets out how Newcastle City Council (referred to as the 'Council') will support increasing uptake of electric vehicles (referred to as 'EV') on roads across the city. This strategy has a 5 year time horizon. Newcastle City Council (the Council) has provided a range of public charge points for Electric Vehicles (EVs) since 2015. The Council's vision is to create a leading network of charging infrastructure in neighbourhoods and city destinations that will support and accelerate the transition towards EVs. There are 5 proposed Priority Actions in the strategy covering a range of charging infrastructure scenarios across the city - they are: -Action 1: Deliver an inclusive neighbourhood charge point roll-out -Action 2: Establish a network of publicly available destination EV charge points -Action 3: Deliver an EV car club model -Action 4: Accelerate EV transition within the Council and Your Homes Newcastle fleet-Action 5: Deploy rapid charging infrastructure for electric taxis. column19: The Byker housing scheme was constructed in the 1970s and covers an area of approximately 80 hectares, comprising residential properties and community buildings. One of the most notable features is the Byker Wall, a 2km long continuous block of multi-storey maisonettes along the north boundary of the estate which contains 620 homes. The rest of the estate generally consists of a mixture of low-rise multi-storey blocks and terraced housing, all characterised by modernist architecture with the use of bright colours. There is one high-rise cluster to the north- western corner. Apart from some privately-owned houses, all of the estate and some community buildings is heated by the Byker district heating scheme (referred to as the Byker Heat Network). Newcastle City Council, together with project partners (Karbon Homes, Byker Community Trust and Your Homes Newcastle) is currently conducting a Strategic Feasibility Study for the Decarbonisation, Renewal and Reconfiguration of the Byker Heat Network. The purpose of this strategic feasibility study is to: a)Conduct an independent investigation into and an analysis of the causes of the primary side network failures that took place in late 2021 b)Undertake a detailed condition assessment of the primary side network including recommendations for repairs and renewals of end-of-life elements c)Assess the potential routes to full decarbonisation of the heat network d)Undertake a techno economic appraisal of the technologies available to achieve the decarbonisation e)Examine the options for the conversion and reconfiguration of the primary distribution network such that is compatible with those potential low carbon options identified in c b) and incorporate renewal of end-of-life elements of the network as identified in b) (expected to be most significantly the primary network and the back-up oil-fired boilers) f)Undertake an appraisal of potential alternative energy centre location(s) to the single Byker Heat Station which currently supplies heat to the network, and thereby improve system resilience g)Examine the potential expansion opportunities to the heat network including new and existing properties h)Provide an economic assessment (including capital costs, operational and maintenance costs, and lifecycle costs) of the potential scheme options identified in ca) to ge) and identify routes to funding such scheme.

Tyne Rivers Trust is leading a project that aims to reduce the fine sediment load of the South Tyne by at least 20% while reducing lead and zinc contamination. Using nature based solutions the work will also contribute to improved water quality, natural flood management, habitat restoration and carbon sequestration. An aligned project promoting regenerative farming will maximise the impact of the project while improving soil health, increasing carbon capture and water retention. 
The first phase of the project has been completed. This was a fine sediment fingerprinting study that was funded by Northumbrian Water and the Mining Remediation Authority, and delivered by Tyne Rivers Trust and Rothamsted Research. Through the study key locations were identified along the South Tyne where interventions to tackle fine sediment pollution will have the greatest impact. This has enabled identifying Wellhope Burn as a priority for the next phase of the project. 

Using measures such as riverbank stabilisation, woodland and wetland creation, ditch blocking and reconnecting the river to its floodplain and natural course, the pilot project will reduce the South Tyne fine sediment load by approximately 3.3%, reduce heavy metal load by approximately 1 tonne per year, create 7 hectares of woodland, 1 hectare of wetlands and ponds and lead to restoration of 2.5 hectares of floodplain. 


Project information and costs/investment costs have been obtained from information on the Carbon and Nature Marketplace. Further information is available on the link provided.

Large scale external fabric retrofit programme - Nottingham has around 5,500 solid brick or system built council houses that require external wall insulation and other fabric energy efficiency measures, and could benefit from solar PV on roofs.

Nottingham has been pioneering approaches utilising modern construction methods, such as panelisation and offsite manufacture through its Energiesprong programme, to deliver deep retrofit with high quality, guaranteed performance and low disruption to occupiers. However, these approaches need delivery at scale to truly realise their potential and drive down costs.

A programme at the scale of 1,000 properties per year would be a game changer in driving the development of a new locally-based industry to manufacture and install high quality external wall insulation and other measures, using modern construction methods and offsite manufacture.

Based on Nottingham's experience, there is currently a funding gap in the order of £25k between the cost of offsite manufacture external fabric measures and the investment that can be justified based on long-term maintenance savings, property value increases and other revenues. This will decrease through economies of scale and innovation in approach.

Given Nottingham's experience and current programme, and its in-depth knowledge of the supply chain, it is very well place to scale up fast. Our current projects have shown a lack of capacity and capability in the supply chain to deliver the required solutions at a cost effective price point, so our programme will need to start scaling up gradually, with a target of achieving 1000 per year once capacity is built.

Over the next 10+ years, Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) will invest over $500+ million in water management (e.g., drainage) and water quality improvement (Superfund cleanup, combined sewer overflows control, source control sufficiency, etc.) infrastructure in the Duwamish Valley. Additionally, SPU will begin planning, designing, and delivery of flooding prevention infrastructure projects to protect the Duwamish Valley community—residents and businesses—from the impacts of extreme precipitation, high tides, and rising sea levels. Given the financial restrictions and need for utility nexus on spending ratepayer dollars, investments from SPU alone will not create transformative change and placemaking for the community. However, through creating alignment, with community, other government agencies and funders, the design of SPU investments can facilitate positive community outcomes.
Our planning and delivery of these projects will also focus on developing replicable and scalable community investment and engagement models suitable for our local and regional context.

ADDITIONAL CONTEXT
This 685 acre area is currently home to 4,154 residents and 6,426 jobs. It is the center of the City's Latino community with a population that is 47% Latino and more than 70% of residents are non-white. Median household income is 40% below the Seattle average with a third of residents below 200% of the poverty level. Due to historic land use practices and decisions, this area has disproportionate health inequities, environmental burdens; area residents have 13-year shorter life expectancy than other, wealthier and less diverse, areas of Seattle. The area is home to Seattle's only river and the City's largest Superfund site. If unaddressed, flooding related to climate change will threaten both industry and small residential parts of the community. At present, South Park experiences flooding associated with heavy rainfall with increased flooding due to both the sea-level rise and rainfall intensity impacts of climate change. Of the 120 acres in Seattle projected to experience daily water levels in 2060 that are 2' greater than today's high tide, the majority are located in the South Park industrial area. The defined outputs of this effort will contribute to improved health and avoid negative outcomes for both the residents and businesses. The water infrastructure will reduce the existing flooding in South Park associated with flooding from rainfall and deliver new infrastructure to manage the expected flooding associated with sea level rise and the rising Duwamish River. The management of sea level rise, delivered in a community-centered manner, will also address needed open space buffering for residents living in the industrial area, contributing positively to public health outcomes for those residents. Second, it provides an opportunity to bring together and leverage the investment of others including the Army Corps of Engineers, Port of Seattle, King County, US Forest Service, affordable housing providers, private property owners, community foundations, nonprofits, etc. Collaboration of that scale between government agencies working in South Park is unprecedented and will allow capital and program investments to be planned and delivered strategically rather than in individual government silos.

Belfast Retrofit Delivery Hub was established in September 2022 following the Belfast Net Zero Carbon Roadmap identifying buildings and transport as the two highest carbon emitting sectors in Belfast. The Hub takes a consortium approach to catalyse retrofit activity across the public and private building sectors in Belfast, engaging stakeholders from across the construction supply chain, funders, academics, public bodies, housing providers and consumer bodies. The Hub's work is informed by the National Retrofit Strategy produced by the Construction Leadership Council. 

There are almost 150,000 homes in the city of Belfast, half of them owned by the people who live in them. Terraced and semi-detached properties make up more than two thirds of the city's homes and mains gas dominates heating supply. Public, commercial and industrial buildings are also major players, accounting for almost a third of the city's emissions and just under a fifth of its energy spend each year. The city's commitment to tackling climate change means that these same homes need to be Net Zero by 2050. 
Belfast City Council has commissioned the Energy Systems Catapult to produce a Local Area Energy Plan (LAEP), which is a data-driven approach to map and model the whole energy system across the city covering production, consumption, demand. The process collates, for the first time, valuable data about housing stock condition, single glazing, Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs) and energy demand, highlighting that 63%of homes have an Energy Performance Certificate rating of D-G. LAEP priority projects include transitioning 500 homes from oil to low carbon heating systems supporting the retrofit of up to 2,000 homes through a cross tenure, area based retrofit programme.

From Waste to Value: A Garden Waste Diversion Initiative in Johannesburg

Context and Purpose
Garden waste makes up a significant portion of Johannesburg's municipal waste stream. Traditionally, this organic material has been sent to landfills, contributing to methane emissions, groundwater contamination, and public health risks. Recognizing the environmental and economic costs of this approach, the City of Johannesburg is exploring sustainable alternatives to transform garden waste from a liability into a resource.

 Strategic Vision
The initiative aims to:
- Reduce landfill pressure and associated health risks
- Lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions
- Create value through composting, mulching, biochar, and energy recovery
- Promote community participation and workforce inclusion in green jobs
Waste Diversion Pathways

The project outlines multiple pathways for garden waste processing:

- Drop-off & Collection: Community-based systems for gathering garden waste
- Composting & Mulching: Soil enrichment and urban agriculture support
- Biochar & Energy Recovery: Advanced technologies for carbon sequestration and renewable energy
- Reuse: Creative repurposing of organic materials

Each pathway is designed to maximize environmental returns while fostering local innovation and participation.

 Health Risks of Poor Landfill Management
The initiative also responds to the urgent need to mitigate the health impacts of unmanaged landfill.

 Inclusive Workforce Development
A key component of the project is building a more inclusive green workforce. In 2021, 41% of Conservation Corps participants came from demographic groups historically underrepresented in conservation jobs. The initiative seeks to expand these opportunities, ensuring that environmental stewardship also advances social equity.

Johannesburg's informal settlements lack safe, reliable energy, forcing households to rely on illegal connections and polluting fuels. Solar microgrid: 3 kWh/day per household (432 kWh/day total), with public lighting.
Impact per household/year:
0.35-0.42 tCO₂e avoided
0.7-1.0 kg PM2.5 avoided
R3,300-3,500 saved
Projected Benefits

Pilot (144 households): 110 tCO₂e + 0.25 t PM2.5 avoided/year.
City-wide (249,000 households): 95,400 tCO₂e + 172,450 kg PM2.5 avoided/year.
Case study (Amarasta): 2.65 MW solar, R60m cost, 18-month payback, 80 jobs created.

Equity & Health Gains
Lower costs for the poorest households.
Reduced exposure to air pollution, especially for women and children.
More time for education, work, and social activities.

The Municipality of Athens will develop an energy
community to produce clean energy and distribute it to citizens and, above all, to vulnerable households. The initial phase of the community will be implemented in the

2) Supply of energy products, devices, and services to its members, with the aim of reducing energy consumption and the use of conventional fuels as well as improving energy efficiency.
3) Promotion of electrification and supply for its members of electric vehicles, hybrid or otherwise, and in general vehicles that use alternative fuels.
4) Demand-side management to reduce the final use of electricity and representation of producers and consumers in the electricity market.
5) Network development, management, and exploitation of alternative fuel infrastructure or management of sustainable means of transport.

The Municipality is currently targeting the purchase of the first 20 MW. The total installed capacity required to achieve the Municipality's strategic priority for electricity produced by energy communities is approximately 270

column19: Las malas prácticas de conducción de un vehículo automotor inciden en su eficiencia energética. Se ha demostrado que los altos tiempos en ralentí, aceleraciones y frenadas bruscas, operación del motor a altas revoluciones por minuto (RPM), uso de accesorios como el aire acondicionado, estado técnico-mecánico deficiente; guardan una relación directa con el consumo de combustible y sus emisiones atmosféricas asociadas. Es así como, en los últimos años ha emergido el concepto de la conducción sostenible, como una estrategia a corto plazo, por medio de la cual se busca reducir el consumo energético de los vehículos, así como disminuir el riesgo por accidentalidad y reducir costos en la operación de los vehículos. Por lo anterior, se ha considerado implementar un programa de conducción sostenible que permita maximizar los beneficios en calidad del aire, seguridad vial y económicos, por parte de los conductores de la ciudad

En ese sentido, las entidades territoriales junto a los Centros de Diagnóstico Automotor les compete la implementación del etiquetado, asimismo al Distrito le corresponde establecer acciones de control y seguimiento como pico y placa según el nivel de etiqueta, acceso a zonas de bajas y cero emisiones, corredores verdes, entre otros, con el fin de unificar la herramienta de etiquetado con las acciones de incentivo al uso de tecnologías más limpias. Para el año 2022 se espera contar con la clasificación de etiquetado a nivel nacional y a nivel distrital se espera contar con un piloto de etiquetado vehicular, posteriormente se espera actualizar las restricciones en circulación y demás programas que puedan utilizar los niveles de etiqueta ambiental como instrumento de categorización. Esto facilitará el control en vía y las políticas de restricciones vehiculares, que en la actualidad están definidas para vehículos particulares según el número de la placa, que pueden ser exentos de las restricciones en circulación si se paga una tarifa plena independientemente del impacto en la calidad del aire de la tecnología que circula. Para vehículos de carga pesada las restricciones actuales se llevan a cabo según la capacidad de carga y año modelo de circulación, e históricamente del 2019 hacia atrás se tenía un pico y placa ambiental de una hora diaria según la placa.A lo largo del tiempo se busca que la cantidad de vehículos con etiquetas de cero y bajas emisiones aumente en la ciudad, asimismo, que las etiquetas con niveles asociados de emisiones mayores se reduzcan, logrando así una disminución de las emisiones totales por el parque automotor que circula en la ciudad.

column15: Control en vía de fuentes móviles mediante la implementación de sensores remotos
column17: Project not funded and seeking partial funding
column18: Public finance- own budget|Loans from International Financial Institutions
column19: Una de las estrategias para aumentar la cobertura en el control a fuentes móviles y determinar su estado ambiental bajo condiciones reales de operación, es a través el uso de sistemas telemáticos de control, tales como sensores remotos, que aumenta ostensiblemente el número de vehículos probados y presenta resultados de emisiones típicas de la operación. Esta tecnología es similar a las cámaras salvavidas que detectan excesos de velocidad, pero centrado en la detección de emisiones de contaminantes en condiciones reales de operación vehicular. En el caso de la SDA, en el año 2019, se realizaron pruebas piloto con sensores remoto bajo condiciones reales de operación, éste estudio y otros de la literatura, muestran que es una opción viable para aumentar la cobertura y el seguimiento ambiental vehicular en el parque automotor, sin embargo hay retos a solucionar para su aplicación en la ciudad, tales como:-Normatividad: No hay límites de emisión establecidos para llevar a cabo el control por este método y que sea comparable a una medición convencional en vía. Por otra parte, no está regulado los comparendos electrónicos para mediciones ambientales.-Estandarización: No hay un marco de estandarización de este tipo de métricas a nivel nacional.-Tecnológico: Es un método que se encuentra en proceso de desarrollo a nivel mundial, por lo cual pueden haber variaciones tecnológicas en los métodos de medición y en las métricas. -Operativo: Se debe definir el marco operativo del control por sensores remotos, asociando un personal operativo para garantizar la continuidad en las mediciones, la fiscalización y el análisis de los resultados. así como la definición de puntos de medición, entre otros parámetros.-Económico: Es necesario establecer qué es más apropiado para llevar a cabo el control por sensores remotos, a partir de una tercerización o a partir de la compra de equipos de medición propios de la ciudad.-Integración: Hay un reto de integración de los datos obtenidos y los sistemas de información y de tecnología de la SDA y de la ciudad.Por lo anterior, es necesario resolver cada una de las incógnitas, por tanto, se propone una fase de un segundo piloto, y en el caso positivo de una evaluación viable en cada uno de los componentes del control, se continúa con la fase de implementación, para así lograr en el 2023 un control real en la ciudad utilizando esta tecnología cuyo potencial contempla un incremento de 20 veces la cobertura de vehículos probados.

column19: Objetivo: Realizar un ascenso tecnológico en la maquinaria de construcción que opera en la ciudad, para reducir sus aportes dematerial particulado y gases generados por la combustión interna de sus motoresDescripción: Las emisiones generadas por la operación de maquinaria de construcción no se encuentran reguladas en el país, lo queimplica que ingresen maquinaria nueva o usada que no son homologadas por estándares internacionales como los definidospor las normativas Tier y Stage, que buscan reducir consumos de combustibles y emisiones atmosféricas mediante laimplementación de tecnologías más eficientes y amables con el medio ambiente. Esta situación implica que las maquinariasque se comercializan y operan en la ciudad no llegan a cumplir con los estándares mínimos reglamentados a nivel mundial,evidenciado rezagos tecnológicos. Por otra parte, una gran proporción operan con motores ciclo diésel y han superado sutiempo de vida útil, situación que no favorece la calidad del aire de la ciudad.De acuerdo con lo anterior, el resultado busca establecer un estándar mínimo de emisión que deben cumplir toda maquinarianueva o usada que opere en la ciudad. Para lo cual, se definió que, a partir del 01 de enero del año 2023, los importadoresy/o ensambladores deben garantizar que sus maquinarias cumplan con el estándar Tier 4i, o su equivalente, Stage IIIB. Conlo que, se planteó un ascenso tecnológico escalonado a implementarse entre los años 2021 y 2030, tomando como criterioque actualmente todas las maquinarias cumplen con estándar de emisión TierI. Así las cosas, para el escenario optimista seplanteó que al año 2030 el 80% del parque automotor cumplirá con el estándar definido. En el escenario intermedio, el 60%,y en el escenario pesimista, el 20%. Para la ejecución del resultado se definieron las siguientes actividades: 1) Inventario ycaracterización de maquinaria, 2) selección y evaluación de requisito mínimo tecnológico, 3) regulación de implementaciónde requisito mínimo, 4) regulación incentivos económicos y financieros, 5, implementación del requisito mínimo. Impactos: • Ambientales: Reducciones de emisiones estimadas para los contaminantes: NOx y PM10.• Salud: Reducción en el número de muertes atribuidas por la exposición de concentración de PM2.5• Económicos: Ahorro en los costos asociados a la reducción de muertes atribuidas Presupuesto Estimado: 11697 millones de pesos colombianos

In this model, some, or all, of the electric bus parts manufactured by a third party will be leased by the public passenger transport system operator. The parts to be rented can be batteries or the whole bus. The bus operator will pay a flat monthly fee to the lessor based on specific conditions, possibly with a monthly surcharge based on the distance traveled. If the battery-only model is adopted, the upfront cost for electric buses will be significantly reduced and almost equivalent to the cost of buying a traditional diesel bus. As a result, the bus operator can purchase an electric bus without incurring any additional additional costs than usual. The transfer of operational risk and technology from the operator to the lessor will also facilitate fleet electrification.

The site is technically well suited, but its inner-city location requires the building to be integrated attractively into the urban landscape. The aim is to upgrade this previously underused area, which is surrounded by traffic. The urban development concept envisages breaking up the area with several buildings featuring attractive, green façades. The idea of planning a small restaurant at the facility was also well received. There are also discussions about connecting the area to the Neckar river. The heat pump extracts up to five degrees of heat from the water taken from the Neckar. The temperature of the Neckar may not fall by more than one degree Celsius in total. This value is calculated by relating the cooled water volume to the volume flow of the Neckar. The plant will fall well below this legally prescribed value: when in operation, it will cool the Neckar by a total of around 0.3 degrees Celsius.
The wastewater heat pump will be built near the North Wastewater Treatment Plant in Neuenheimer Feld. Although the urban planning requirements here are less demanding than for the river heat pump, an attractive architectural concept has also been developed for this project: the plan is to construct a building whose visual design implies the waves of the Neckar River.
The heat pump will use the heat from the wastewater. The temperature of wastewater from households is higher than that of the Neckar, especially in the winter months. This means that the heat pump can cool the wastewater by up to seven degrees Celsius.
The heat pumps increase the temperature of the heat extracted from the river or wastewater to approx. 90 to 95 degrees Celsius, so that the heat can be fed into the district heating network. Each of the two plants will generate 130,000 to 240,000 megawatt hours of usable heat per year at an output of 30 megawatts. The plants are scheduled to go into operation by 2029.

column19: Under this action, Lagos State will undertake an evaluation of the cur- rent status of waste management and develop a Waste Infrastructure Development Strategy by 2022. The evaluation will be based on data on tons of waste collected, waste composition and volumes processed by MRF and composting facilities. The strategy will aim to increase the capacity of Lagos's waste transfer, material recovery, bio- digester and composting facilities. It will mandate the construction of new waste infrastructure, including transfer loading stations, starting in Iberekodo, Agunlejika and Odogunyan. The strat- egy will build on the progress the State has made so far in establishing waste transfer stations and expanding the waste vehicle fleet. The new facilities will need to have the capacity to absorb the expected increase in the volume of recyclables diverted from landfill due to the launch of the Lagos Recycling Initiative. Implementation of the strat- egy is expected to require State funding and cooperation with the private sector through PPPs. The State could institute a levy on waste disposal to support infrastructure investments. A number of previous projects were abandoned because their operation was deemed unfeasible; demand must be confirmed in the planning phase and consideration must be given to how these projects can be made sustainable in the long term. For wastewater management, the State Government intends to develop an Outline Business Case (OBC) study and WIDP for the sector. The OBC study/ WIDP will cover the preparation of detailed engineering designs, drawings and specifications, construction and operational cost estimates, environ- mental and social impact assessments, and analysis of required land use for wastewater infrastructure provision for existing and projected population of the State, in line with Regional Masterplan of the State. The WIDP will further determine project implementation and phasing plan, set timelines and process to be followed for project procurement (either through government funding or through private sector participation), while the OBC study will specifically provide a well-developed and compre- hensive suite of project documents that will be made available to private inves- tors during the procurement process. This is a useful tool that will bring all the elements of the project together, so that any conflicts between factors can be resolved before approaching the pri- vate sector. This document will be used to form the basis on which the project will be assessed and approved for com- mencement of the procurement phase. It will also have served as an investment document to engender the interest of investors and facilitate the implemen- tation of wastewater treatment projects through public private partnerships (PPP) procurement routes. In addition to this, all existing wastewater treat- ment infrastructure in the State will be upgraded and expanded to cover more catchment areas, these include Alausa wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), Abesan WWTP, Oke-Afa WWTP and Iponri WWTP.

The project has been selected by the National Public Employment Service (SEPE) and granted ECODES the appropriate funding for its development.
The aim of this project is to ensure that 64 unemployed citizens (young refugees) in the municipality of Madrid, benefit, after a professional training process, from a first work experience in a segment of the labor market where there is currently a great demand for professionals.
Through the “Emplea T Verde Project”, which has the support of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, UNHCR-Spain, the aim is to achieve a triple impact: 

1.Re-qualification and accompaniment towards green jobs for young people in a situation of unemployment.
2.Adaptation to climate change connecting with the climate strategy of the municipality and specifically with the following lines of work in the buildings subject to the action:
- The improvement of energy efficiency with one or more of these elements: by replacing windows, green surface or improving insulation.
- The installation of renewable energies.
3.Advice on energy efficiency to the residents of the neighborhood where the action is carried out, as well as environmental education programs if any intervention is carried out in schools.

Likewise, as a result of the “Emplea T Verde Project”, the city of Madrid and its citizens will benefit from the actions of energy advice to the citizens and sustainable rehabilitation carried out in public spaces.

Forestami is the project promoted by the Metropolitan City of Milan, the Municipality of Milan, the Lombardy Region, Parco Nord Milano, Parco Agricolo Sud Milano, ERSAF and Fondazione di Comunità Milano, which envisages the planting of 3 million trees by 2030, to increase natural capital, clean the air, improve life in greater Milan and combat the effects of climate change.
The collaboration between all the promoters has allowed us to build a strategic vision on the role of greenery in the Milan metropolitan area; and to give life to a process of census, valorization and implementation of all the green, permeable and tree-lined systems, to promote policies and projects to promote urban forestry activities and build a Metropolitan Park in the Milan area. 
The cost of this measure may vary due to the specific characteristics of the areas to reforest and to the maintenance costs of the tree species. The aim of the project is to ensure that the population of the metropolitan area of Milan benefits from the positive ecosystem impacts of the reforestation program, from health benefits, to mitigation and water retention.
As of the agronomic season 2023/2024, the project has already planted 611.459 plants and trees in the Metropolitan City of Milano: 
-	58,534 were planted in 29 municipalities of the Metropolitan City directly from Forestami thanks to donations from private citizens and companies. 
-	13,100 plants were planted thanks to the SUPERB project (a European project Horizon 2020 by the University of Milan and Parco Nord Milano). The intervention involved, in the last two agronomic seasons (22-23 and 23-24), a total area of 15.22 hectares distributed among 4 Municipalities of the Metropolitan City of Milan;
-	7,800 trees and shrubs were planted, instead, by the National Biodiversity Future Centre (NBFC), in collaboration with the University of Milan-Bicocca, the Polytechnic of Milan and ERSAF - Lombardy Region. The intervention involved 3 Municipalities on a total area of 3.70 hectares in the agronomic season 23-24;

In the framework of the EU Mission 100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities, in March 2024 the City of Milan developed its Climate City Contract (CCC), including a Commitments document, an Action Plan and an Investment Plan. The Investment Plan outlines: 1. current state of climate investments 2. quantification of the funds needed to implement the CCC actions, highlighting the gap with investments and funding already acquired 3. cost scenario, with the breakdown of expenditure up to 2030, including those underway. 
The total costs of the planned interventions amount to approximately 6 billion euros investments, of which 2.6 billion by the Municipality of Milan and 3.3 billion by the signatory stakeholders.
The process of costing all actions involved internal dialogues within the Municipality as well as discussions with stakeholders. This multi-stakeholder approach added complexity to the process, as it required alignment of diverse interests and priorities. Furthermore, the emphasis on actions made possible by access to extraordinary EU funding introduced uncertainties regarding the availability and allocation of funds. The resulting portfolio of actions comprises a mix of clearly defined projects, some related to specific areas and sites, and others pertaining to the entire city or network infrastructure. This diversity in scope made the process even more complex, as each action requires a tailored approach. Additionally, enabling actions that support mitigation actions (e.g. citizen engagement) presented by both the Municipality and stakeholders contribute to a further 10% reduction in emissions. 
Priority areas of action include energy requalification of buildings, new infrastructures, tools aimed at promoting soft mobility, depaving, new plantings, reclamation and innovative projects for citizen involvement.

Paris has made the decision to establish a carbon offset operator as part of its efforts to accelerate the ecological transition. This initiative aims to support individuals, businesses, and local authorities seeking to offset their greenhouse gas emissions by financing environmentally beneficial projects. The operator takes the form of a cooperative, bringing together various stakeholders such as companies, experts, NGOs, and project developers, all working towards the common objective of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. 

To encompass a wide range of sectors, the operator will utilize multiple financing tools including a low-carbon label, energy saving certificates, and crowdfunding. These resources will be directed towards initiatives in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, forestry, energy-efficient building renovations, and more. 

For instance, the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games, which aim to be carbon-neutral, attracted 600 000 € of compensation, as Paris 2024 has opted to finance projects in France through the Low Carbon Label.
(https://press.paris2024.org/news/paris-2024-presents-the-results-of-its-actions-to-make-the-games-more-sustainable-36aef-7578a.html) 

In order to match the offsetting required to balance the part of the Parisian footprint currently deemed incompressible by 2050, disposing of a local operator and of local offsetting projects will be a pivotal financial mechanisms.

For more information, see the Cooperative Carbone's website.
(https://coopcarbone-parismetropole.fr/les-projets/)

The City of Paris benefits from occasional patronage on a project to project basis. The Paris 2024 fund, created for the Olympics, established solid partnerships, potentially interested for patronage opportunity beyond 2024 in order to contribute to the investments needed for the betterment of Paris and its ecological planning in order to become a low carbon and resilient territory.

The Council of Paris therefore approved in October 2024 the principle of creating a patronage fund titled 'Paris 2050'. 
(https://a06-v7.apps.paris.fr/a06/jsp/site/plugins/solr/modules/ods/DoDownload.jsp?id_document=176945&items_per_page=20&sort_name=&sort_order=&terms=dotation%202050&query=dotation%202050)

First and foremost, Paris 2050 will be a distributive and participatory fund, aiming to promote and develop public policies led by the City of Paris and thus finance, in compliance with the City's Ethical Charter for Patronage and Sponsorship, innovative projects pursuing a general interest, particularly in the ecological transition and in the fields of sport, culture, social, education, heritage, and philanthropy. These projects may be implemented by City departments or by any non-profit organization in the Paris region for initiatives supported by the City.

Its governance will be ensured by a Board of Directors comprising three committees composed of four representatives each: a committee representing the City of Paris, a committee of patrons, and a committee of qualified individuals.

The Board of Directors will be assisted by an Investment Committee, which will provide opinions and recommendations on investment policy and may propose studies and expertise. Finally, in order to maintain a certain flexibility of action, the Mayor of Paris will only approve the most structural projects [which will concern only the Parisian community]: projects exceeding one million euros, or an amount lower than requested by at least two members of the City's college of representatives.

The organization and operation of the fund are detailed in the draft statutes annexed to this resolution and will be supplemented in internal regulations to be adopted subsequently by the fund's board of directors.

column19: O Distrito de Baixa Emissão-DBE constitui na implantação, até 2030, de uma zona de baixa emissão de GEE na Cidade, com promoção de espaços urbanos de qualidade, com foco na melhoria da qualidade de vida e da saúde e da qualidade do ar, resultando em um ambiente mais atrativo, através de ações que tem como base incremento da infraestrutura verde, a requalificação urbana resiliente e sustentável dos espaços públicos, considerando a implementação de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza como jardins de chuva, canteiros pluviais, pavimentos permeáveis, arborização (sombreamento e eficiente na filtragem do ar), o incentivo ao transporte limpo, à mobilidade ativa, através de ciclovia, travessias elevadas, melhoria de acessibilidade, uso de tecnologias limpas relativas a iluminação e sinalização e ações complementares compensatórias, inclusive relativas a edificações e resíduos. O Distrito de Baixa Emissão, criado e coordenado pelo Escritório de Planejamento da Subsecretaria de Planejamento e Acompanhamento de Resultados da Secretaria de Fazenda e Planejamento, está alinhado com o Decreto Municipal \'Ruas Verdes e Saudáveis\' (Decreto Rio no. 46.081/2019) e com o Plano de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Ação Climática (PDS) da Cidade do Rio. Em 2021 o Distrito foi instituído pela Lei Complementar Nº 229/2021. No Plano Estratégico da Cidade para os anos entre 2021 e 2024, o Distrito de Baixa Emissão-DBE é estabelecido como uma das metas estratégicas. Conforme previsto na Lei Complementar Nº 229/2021, o DBE foi regulamentado pelo Decreto Rio Nº 51047/2022. O Distrito, com uma área de 2,34 Km², está localizado na Região Administrativa do Centro do Rio de Janeiro, que inclui os bairros do Centro e da Lapa, que juntos possuem uma população de moradores de aproximadamente 32.758, de acordo com o senso de 2012. Ainda deve-se considerar a população flutuante na área. A delimitação do DBE considera área com forte centralidade, alta concentração de serviços, comércio e empresas, intenso fluxo de pedestre e veículos. Destaca-se ainda nesta área, fatores como: a existência de modos de transportes não poluentes, como VLT e Metro, sua localização entre dois polos de transporte (Central do Brasil e Praça Quinze), e a existência de áreas históricas e diversas vias peatonais de grande fluxo, onde os benefícios do projeto podem alcançar grande número de pessoas. Desta forma o projeto e sua implementação, tem grande potencial de trazer benefícios tanto ambientais como sócio econômico, podendo ser um grande exemplo que estimule novas soluções para promoção da resiliência e de qualidade urbana no centro, gerando um ambiente urbano mais saudável para as pessoas que moram ou transitam pela região Central, e benefícios indiretos como redução de problemas de saúde relacionados à poluição do ar, aumento da ocupação da área Central (comercial e residencial) e estímulo ao mercado de energia limpa. Até o momento foram elaborados planos de monitoramento da Qualidade do Ar e de GEE, plano de comunicação, implantados alguns trechos de ciclovias, elaborado estudo preliminar para requalificação urbana de uma avenida no DBE, está em andamento estudos para traçar estratégias de transição para transporte de carga zero emissões.

column19: O Município do Rio de Janeiro, ao promover a extensiva alteração dos espaços naturais e a não priorização da implantação de espaços livres/verdes, compromete a prestação de uma gama de serviços ambientais, a exemplo da preservação dos recursos hídricos, manutenção da estabilidade de encostas, o arrefecimento do calor intraurbano e a conservação de áreas verdes urbanas que promovem bem-estar e o convívio social. Em meio a este contexto, as atividades de monitoramento ambiental se mostram cada vez mais relevantes e são de extrema importância para o planejamento e gestão do território em prol de cidades sustentáveis e da busca por justiça ambiental. O monitoramento da cobertura vegetal fornece informações sobre os fatores que influenciam o estado de conservação, preservação, degradação e recuperação ambiental da área estudada. Também subsidia medidas de planejamento e controle e auxilia na definição de políticas públicas ambientais. O bioma Mata Atlântica, protegido pela Lei nº 11.428/2006 (Lei da Mata Atlântica) e por diferentes categorias de Unidades de Conservação é pressionado pelo processo de expansão da malha urbana da cidade do Rio de Janeiro, se tornando cada vez mais fragmentado, apresentando uma distribuição espacial desigual entre os bairros das diferentes áreas de planejamento, ocasionando a perda de biodiversidade e da qualidade de vida da população. Através do levantamento sistemático, contínuo e amplo de dados relativos à cobertura vegetal do município, o Programa de Monitoramento Contínuo da Cobertura Vegetal busca gerar informações espaciais e índices ambientais que permitam a elaboração de uma base de dados espaço-temporal que evidencia as mudanças relacionadas à cobertura vegetal da cidade. O banco de dados gerado permite que os órgãos municipais tenham um instrumento de gestão seguro e preciso para tomada de decisões nas áreas de fiscalização, licenciamento ambiental, conservação da biodiversidade, restauração ambiental e adaptação às mudanças climáticas. O banco de dados contendo os valores cadastrais de cada fisionomia mapeada em escala de detalhe encontra-se disponível a partir de um SIG Web que pode ser consultado em https://www.data.rio/app/sig-floresta. O mapeamento da cobertura vegetal fornece subsídios ao alcance de atividades e metas relacionadas à mitigação e adaptação da cidade aos eventos climáticos extremos como por exemplo: Enquadramento de novas áreas verdes como áreas protegidas; Manutenção e aprimoramento de um banco de dados com informações atualizadas sobre os programas de ação e recuperação ambiental da cidade do Rio de Janeiro; Diagnóstico das áreas prioritárias para o reflorestamento e; Controle dos fatores que impulsionam o avanço da malha urbana sobre a Mata Atlântica. São diretrizes do PMCV i) Uso de geotecnologias para apoio à aquisição e tratamento de dados; ii) Construção de indicadores e índices para apoio ao planejamento e gestão da cobertura vegetal; iii) Mapeamento e Classificação das áreas verdes do município de acordo com suas fitofisionomias; iv) Identificação periódica da composição das espécies e estrutura vegetal das comunidades e ecossistemas presentes no município; v) Análise espaço-temporal das áreas verdes para melhor compreensão do processo de uso e ocupação do solo e; vi) Monitoramento das políticas públicas de proteção, conservação, restauração e compensação relacionadas à cobertura vegetal. São alguns dos objetivos específicos do PMCV: i) Sistematizar informações relativas às características da cobertura vegetal da cidade; ii) Monitorar a dinâmica de transformação da paisagem no que tange à cobertura vegetal da cidade e; iii) Subsidiar ações governamentais de mitigação e adaptação da cidade relativas a manutenção do equilíbrio ecológico dos ecossistemas associados ao Bioma Mata Atlântica na Cidade. Por fim, os produtos do PMCV estão relacionados ao mapeamento, classificação, quantificação, avaliação espacial e temporal, e registro e divulgação de dados referentes à cobertura vegetal do município. Esses produtos permitem a aplicação de uma série de ações como a definição de áreas prioritárias para conservação e recuperação da Mata Atlântica; proposição de implantação de corredores verdes; realização de estudos de inventário arbóreo; estimativa dos estoques de carbono nos ecossistemas do Rio; planejamento do uso e ocupação do solo e a dinâmica de transformação da paisagem; cálculo dos índices de áreas verdes (m2/hab.) em diferentes recortes municipais; elaboração de estudos para criação de Unidades de Conservação e planos de manejo desses territórios e; análises espaciais voltadas para o licenciamento e fiscalização ambiental.

column19: El Código Rojo es un protocolo que busca instalar y visibilizar el riesgo de calor extremo tanto de cara a la ciudadanía como en los servicios públicos que son los llamados a generar acciones para enfrentarlo. La primera versión se lanzó el 14 de diciembre de 2022 y será actualizado año a año para que sea cada vez más robusto.Este es el resultado del trabajo realizado con la fuerza de tarea de Calor Extremo en la que participan instituciones tanto del nivel regional como central: Gobierno Regional Metropolitano de Santiago, Delegación Presidencial, Dirección Regional de ONEMI, Dirección Meteorológica de Chile, Secretaría Regional Ministerial de Salud, Secretaría Regional Ministerial de Desarrollo Social y Familia, Secretaría Regional Ministerial de Trabajo y Previsión Social y Secretaría Regional Ministerial de Educación.Cobertura: El protocolo se extiende a toda la Región Metropolitana.La activación de las alertas del protocolo se realiza a partir de la siguiente tabla:· Alerta Verde - Temprana Preventiva: se activará cuando la temperatura pronosticada sea igual o superior a 33°C.· Alerta Amarilla: se activará cuando la temperatura pronosticada sea igual o superior a 34°C.· Alerta Roja: se activará cuando la temperatura pronosticada sea igual o superior a 35°.Cada Secretaría Regional Ministerial genera una serie de acciones y gestiones asociadas a cada alerta para informar y activar sus redes asociadas.El código va asociado a la comunicación del riesgo mediante campañas en redes sociales y prensa con las siguientes recomendaciones:• Beber abundante agua.• Comer alimentos como frutas y verduras.• Usa sombrero o gorra, gafas UV y ropa transpirable.• No exponerse al sol, y de hacerlo, usar protector adecuado.• No beber alcohol.• Toma una ducha con agua fría.• Ponerse paños fríos en el cuello y antebrazos.• Mantén tu hogar más frío que el exterior priorizando ventilación cruzada antes que A/C.• Evitar actividad física entre las 11 y las 18 hrs.Actualmente no se ha dimensionado el costo, hasta el momento solo se aplican medidas de gestión sin recursos para proyectos.

column17: Project partially funded and seeking additional funding
column19: Eastwick is an environmental justice community in Southwest Philadelphia that is vulnerable to multiple sources of flooding, including riverine (historically the source of catastrophic flooding), tidal flooding, and coastal storm surge. With sea level rise, nuisance flooding may also occur in parts of Eastwick. A multi-pronged flood resilience strategy is needed to holistically address current and future flood risk in Eastwick. Residents have been waiting a long time for action to address flooding. Over the years, many partners have come developed various ideas and concepts on how to mitigate flooding in Eastwick. These ideas are in different phases of feasibility and include options like a levee on Cobbs Creek, nature-based solutions, voluntary buyouts, a land swap/relocation plan, and reconstruction of current homes on higher foundations.\nThe Office of Sustainability (OOS) has received funding through FEMA's Flood Mitigation Assistance Program to develop a community driven Flood Resilience Strategy. The Flood Resilience Strategy aims to bring these ideas and partners into one dedicated planning process with Eastwick residents steering decision making on how to move forward. Through engagement of community and agency stakeholders, technical feasibility analysis, and an options evaluation, the project will identify a community-supported preferred comprehensive flood resilience strategy, which will likely include multiple components that work together, and an implementation roadmap for Eastwick. With this roadmap, the project team intends to develop at least one funding application for the implementation of one or a combination of flood resilience measures.\nWhile a long-term strategy is being developed, OOS has secured funding to design and construct an interim flood barrier to provide near-term relief from riverine flooding.

단순히 정책 수립에 그치지 않고, 시민·기업·기관이 모두 참여하는 실행 체계를 통해 감축 성과를 확대합니다.

1. 창원시 탄소중립 지원센터 운영
1)핵심 역할: 지역 내 탄소중립 정책을 총괄·조정하는 허브
2)주요 기능: 탄소중립 기본계획·이행계획 수립 및 평가 지원, 국가·지자체 간 정책 연계 및 국제 대응체계(CDP, GCoM 등) 보고 총괄, 민간기업·시민사회·학계 등과 협력 채널 구축
3)성과 지향점: 행정 일관성 강화, 정책 집행력 제고, 공공의 신뢰 기반 확보

2. 창원시 중소기업 탄소중립 전환 지원
1)대상: 창원시 소재 중소·중견기업
2)지원 방식: 탄소배출 진단 및 컨설팅 제공, 고효율 설비 교체·온실가스 저감 기술 도입 지원, 교육·워크숍을 통한 탄소규제 대응 역량 강화
3)기대효과: 산업부문 배출 저감, 기업 경쟁력 제고(ESG 경영·수출 대응력 강화), 녹색 일자리 창출

3. 창원시 탄소중립 플랫폼 운영 및 시민참여 활성화
1)플랫폼 기능: 시민과 기업이 참여할 수 있는 온라인/오프라인 통합 거버넌스 창구
2)온실가스 인벤토리·정책성과 공개, 시민 탄소발자국 계산·실천 인증 기능, 기업·기관의 참여사례 공유
3)시민참여 활성화 활동 캠페인, 시민 서포터즈, 생활 속 실천 챌린지, 기후교육 콘텐츠 보급
4)기대효과: 시민을 수동적 대상이 아닌 적극적 행동 주체로 전환

4. 창원시 생활실천형 탄소중립 리빙랩 운영
1)리빙랩(Living Lab): 시민, 기업, 연구자, 공공이 실생활 환경에서 직접 실험·검증하는 현장 중심 참여 모델
2)운영 사례: 일회용품 줄이기(주유소 일회용 장갑 시범사업 등), 폐현수막 재활용 파우치 제작·유통, 생활 에너지 절약·자원순환 캠페인
3)기대효과: 시민 생활 속에서 체감 가능한 감축 성과 창출, 정책·기술이 현장에 맞게 조정·확산

Taipei City is advancing solar and renewable energy deployment through multiple initiatives, including landfill-to-energy transformation, the Taipei Solar Rooftop Project, citizen-owned power plants, subsidy programs, and smart grid promotion. By August 2024, the City had installed solar PV systems across 108 municipal agencies and 166 schools, with a total capacity of 49.32 MW. Together with installations by central government and private entities, citywide capacity has reached 81.67 MW, generating an estimated 77.91 million kWh annually and reducing approximately 38,485 tons of CO₂ emissions.

To foster public participation, Taipei pioneered Taiwan's first citizen-owned solar plant on municipal property at Guandu Junior High School in 2020, and continues to open rooftop space for community-led renewable projects. The “Taipei Energy Hill” initiative, repurposing restored landfill sites such as Fudekeng Environmental Restoration Park and Nangang Shanzhulu Eco Park, has added nearly 3 MW capacity and generates 3 million kWh annually under a public-private investment model.

In addition, the City is piloting small hydropower systems, with the first 0.5 kW demonstration plant launched in partnership with private enterprises in 2023. These combined efforts not only enhance renewable energy generation and reduce reliance on fossil fuels but also create opportunities for community engagement, environmental education, and innovative financing models. Taipei City seeks to further scale these initiatives through external financing, ensuring long-term renewable energy resilience and contribution to the City's 2050 Net Zero pathway.

column19: O Projeto Escolas Solares está sendo desenvolvido no âmbito do Programa COMPASSO UFMG, por meio de parceria estabelecida entre a Universidade e Prefeitura de Belo Horizonte, com o objetivo de desenvolver métodos e soluções para áreas municipais mais vulneráveis às mudanças climáticas. O projeto tem como objetivo pesquisar a dinâmica do uso de eletricidade em edificações padrão da rede municipal de ensino, propor ações para a melhoria da eficiência energética de acordo com regulamentos nacionais e preparar a instalação em um sistema solar fotovoltaico gerador interconectado à rede elétrica da concessionária local. Desde setembro de 2018, o projeto Escolas Solares é acelerado pelo Projeto Urban-LEDS II e, desde o final de 2019, integra a iniciativa LEDS Lab deste projeto, ambos financiados pela Comissão Europeia e implementados pelo ICLEI - Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade em parceria com a ONU-Habitat. Neste contexto, Belo Horizonte foi selecionada para receber o apoio direto de um consórcio de consultorias especializadas contratado pelo ICLEI e composto pela Mitsidi Projetos, I Care & Consult, Markup Consultores e Hill Consulting com o objetivo de implementar um projeto piloto de energia fotovoltaica e/ou de eficiência energética a partir de análise de ocupação e de utilização de energia elétrica na Escola Municipal Herbert José de Souza (EMHJS), na região norte, como primeiro passo para implementação do Projeto Escolas Solares.Recentemente, o consórcio de consultorias do LEDS Lab concluiu a série de webinars sobre financiamento climático, dirigida aos membros. Além disso, foram propostas medidas de mitigação a partir das análises realizadas pela UFMG e pela consultoria da iniciativa, que consideram ações de eficiência energética e geração de energia renovável. Duas medidas foram selecionadas por apresentar viabilidade técnica, financeira e ambiental, com vistas a implementá-las na EMHJ, a saber: instalação de sistema de geração de energia solar fotovoltaica (FV); eficientização da iluminação interna, considerando a troca de lâmpadas e luminárias com o objetivo de atender as normas, melhorar o conforto visual e economizar energia.Estas duas medidas de mitigação contarão com o desenvolvimento de um projeto básico para cada, ou seja, elas serão estudadas, orçadas e detalhadas de forma a orientar efetivamente sua execução. Parte destas ações será implementada com o capital semente disponibilizado pelo projeto Urban-LEDSII (EUR 15.000 ou R$ 73.253,00) , e parte será objeto de aplicação para obtenção de financiamento de outras fontes. Recentemente, a consultoria submeteu o projeto Escolas Solares para a chamada PAR-PROCEL, mnão ficando, contudo, entre as finalistas. Na proposta apresentada, foram considerados os custos totais do projeto ou seja, um cenário em que todas as medidas de eficiência energética fossem cumpridas e o sistema de geração de energia solar fotovoltaica fosse integralmente instalado na EMHJS. Além disso, foi considerada a replicação do projeto em dois novos edifícios da rede pública municipal de ensino. Abaixo, são apresentados os custos totais do projeto e os custos de sua replicação:Custos totais EMHJS: R$675.000,00Sistema Fotovoltaico: R$250 000Iluminação: R$130.000,00Troca de equipamentos: R$60.000,00Medidores: R$10 000Retrofit elétrico: R$200 000Capacitação: R$25 000Replicação em 2 edifícios2 pilotos BH (semente): R$134 0002 diagnósticos: R$100 000 (https://www.ufmg.br/espacodoconhecimento/mostrauniversidadecidade/compasso/)

column19: Este projeto é coordenado pela BHTRANS e acelerado, desde setembro de 2018, pelo Projeto Urban LEDS II (implementado pelo ICLEI - Governos Locais pela Sustentabilidade em parceria com a ONU-Habitat com financiamento da Comissão Européia e executado em Belo Horizonte em parceria com a Prefeitura Municipal, por meio da Gerência de Projetos Especiais da Secretaria Municipal do Meio Ambiente), sendo voltado para a eletrificação da frota de transporte público coletivo da capital. A sua visão é a seguinte: \'Em 2021, Belo Horizonte terá uma frota de pelo menos 25 ônibus elétricos operando em seu serviço convencional, com o objetivo de melhorar a qualidade do ar, reduzir a poluição sonora e reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa\'. Para tanto, riscos técnicos, econômicos, comerciais e políticos foram mapeados e ações de mitigação de riscos estão sendo estudadas. As alternativas de financiamento de veículos ou baterias (componentes importados de maior valor) também estão sendo estudadas, mas ainda são um desafio a ser superado. O projeto piloto inclui uma frota de veículos composta por 3 microônibus, 17 ônibus padrão e 5 ônibus articulados. Os microônibus serão alocados ao sistema Vilas e Favelas (aldeias e favelas) e em linhas que circulam nas estradas com restrições à operação de veículos maiores. Eles também podem ser alocados no serviço complementar. Os veículos convencionais e padrão representam a grande maioria da frota municipal, distribuída em linhas circulares, diamétricas, radiais e de alimentação. O uso dos veículos articulados está concentrado no sistema de troncos e eles viajam por rotas exclusivas ou com tratamento preferencial para o transporte público. A redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa, a melhoria da qualidade do ar e a redução da poluição sonora estão entre as oportunidades e os impactos do projeto, bem como o aumento do serviço do sistema de transporte coletivo, com a possibilidade de implementar essa mesma tecnologia em outras áreas. da cidade.

Tendo como elemento central uma árvore, o refúgio contará com uma estrutura concebida a partir de técnicas de resfriamento passivo, contendo um conjunto de pisos permeáveis (gramado e revestimento de micro eixos drenantes). Dessa forma, o cidadão poderá utilizar o refúgio não apenas para se abrigar do sol e reduzir a sensação de calor, mas também para descansar e se hidratar. Ao todo, o refúgio climático ocupará uma área de 25,61 metros quadrados. \nO bebedouro possui tecnologia avançada, com três bicas distintas, destinadas a adultos, crianças e pets. Também possui estações nebulizadoras, com aspersores para dissipar uma névoa refrescante para que o munícipe se alivie do calor. Basta pressionar um dos botões e aguardar a liberação do vapor.

column19: We are currently working with 18 Resiliency Hubs, each with identified Resiliency Hub Leaders that serve as main points of contact with the City. Resiliency Hubs are located in some of the most vulnerable neighborhoods in Baltimore and are a key component of our larger Community Resiliency Planning efforts. Resiliency Hubs are non-profit community organizations, including churches and faith-based organizations, in under-resourced neighborhoods across Baltimore that agree to partner with the city to provide essential resources and community support during times of crisis and emergency, particularly during natural hazard events. They agree to be a trusted community location where vulnerable neighbors can access reliable power for their essential devices, continue to give and receive information as emergency situations develop, store medications sensitive to temperature, and safely congregate until sufficient emergency recovery services arrive, among other things. Resiliency Hubs receive support from the city in many forms including high-quality emergency supplies, energy efficiency improvements to their building, back-up power capabilities (solar and solar storage), emergency response training, connections to grant funding opportunities, and focused support and communications from the Office of Emergency Management, Health Department, and Office of Sustainability. We recently secured $7million+ to convert 16 Hubs t solar energy and install solar backup generators. We are currently working with partners and applying for grants to finance rooftop solar and battery storage projects for Hub use. Additionally, we have and will continue to offer Hub stakeholder convenings and trainings. We would also like to secure a sustainable funding stream to support a small grants program to assist Resiliency Hubs in funding the resources and programs they offer to strengthen community resilience and support their communities during emergencies.
