This proposed programme consists of two phases 

•Phase one consists of two key components, as follows: 1. An updated sea-level rise and extreme wave run-up model for the City of Cape Town consisting of a city-wide assessment of sea-level rise, extreme wave run-up levels, and coastal erosion risk for the present day, mid-future (2050) and far future (2100) periods, taking into account the latest global and local scientific data and updated IPCC climate change scenarios as per AR6. 2. Detailed fine-scale extreme wave run-up models and coastal erosion lines that consider local biophysical factors influential to hazard exposure for the determination of high risk zones for the present day, mid-future and far future periods, taking into account the latest global and local scientific data and updated IPCC climate change scenarios as per AR6. 

•Phase 2 consists of three key components, as follows: 1. Development of a pipeline of coastal resilience infrastructure projects, including both green infrastructure, “grey” infrastructure, and a hybrid approach combining both green and “grey” infrastructure, in response to the results of phase one. 2. A high level technical and financial feasibility assessment for the above pipeline. 3. A business case for investment in coastal resilience infrastructure projects for both the City of Cape Town (to use its own budget) and potential external investors. 

Note: The development of the pipeline of projects must take into account principles of restorative justice in the context of addressing the legacy of apartheid spatial planning through sustainable and risk averse coastal development in areas of need. This aspect is of critical importance to the Cape Flats region of the False Bay coastline, which has been underserviced and under-invested compared to other parts of Cape Town's coastline. 

Due to the value of coastal real estate and the high demand of living along the coastline and benefiting from its resources, coastal mixed-use development is seen as a conduit from which to achieve socio-economic upliftment for coastal communities. Such development does however require that coastal risks are considered to ensure that this development is risk averse and ultimately sustainable over the long term.

The Liveable Urban Waterway Programme (LUW) is a strategic and transversal programme developed by the City of Cape Town in response to the Climate Change Strategy, Water Strategy, Resilience Strategy and Environment Strategy. The programme is rehabilitating various waterways across the city, using water sensitive design, nature-based, and green infrastructure approaches, thereby achieving many benefits for society, the environment and the economy. A number of projects are in planning, development or implementation, and are being implemented by different departments. These are testing different rehabilitation and water sensitive design approaches to demonstrate the shared benefits that nature-based solutions and green infrastructure can provide. 

Projects include: 
1. Sand Langevlei Canals. 
2. Keyser River. 
3. Spaanshemat and Prinskasteel Rivers. 
4. Grootboschkloof River. 
5. Westlake River and Kirstenhof Wetlands. 
6. Vygekraal River. 
7. Asanda Wetland Park. 
8. Upper Kuils River. 
9. Upper Elsieskraal River. 
10. Various waterways in the Diep/Sand catchment. 
11. Various waterways in the Zeekoe catchment. 
12. Adderley Street Canals and Fountain.

 These projects have been designed in collaboration with communities, and to date five co-design workshops and a further 17 community engagements have been undertaken. A project pipeline is in development that has 45 identified projects that could be included under the Liveable Urban Waterway Programme. Work is underway to develop a business case for the investment, package the projects ready for financing and future implementation.

column19: The Cleveland Tree Plan was developed in 2015 by the City of Cleveland in partnership with four non-profits and many additional stakeholders. One of the key tenets of this plan is to treat trees as infrastructure that needs to be invested in. It's clear that the City of Cleveland cannot do this alone, so we are looking for the private sector to step up as well. column19: The City implements a PACE program—Property Assessed Clean Energy program—to finance energy efficiency improvements and renewable energy in buildings. The loan is attached to the property, not the individual or company. Governments or private lenders provide financing to building owners, which helps pay for the upfront costs. Loans are paid back by increasing property taxes by a set rate for an agreed-upon term. Property owners begin saving on energy costs while paying for improvements, often resulting in net gains even with increased property tax.The PACE program is accompanied by an Energy Performance Labeling (EPL) program for some privately owned buildings, which requires public disclosure of energy performance and adherence to minimum standards. Es una acción de cooperación internacional con duración de 3 años (2022-2025), la cual es posible gracias al financiamiento de la Unión Europea y el programa Asociación para ciudades sostenibles.

Es posible conocer más al respecto en: https://metropoliresiliente.imeplan.mx/

column19: Programa de restauração de ecossistemas da UCNs do Recife. A ideia é implementar estratégias e ações de restauração da biodiversidade nas UCNs da Cidade do Recife que já estão elencadas nos Planos de Manejo aprovados e publicados. A ONU declarou essa década como a década da restauração dos ecossistemas. A cidade do Recife pode dar uma grande contribuição para a restauração da biodiversidade uma vez que em seu território existem 25 Unidades de Conservação da Natureza-UCN. Essas UCNs abrigam ecossistemas de Floresta Atlântica e Manguezal, além de possuírem muito habitats alagáveis que são essenciais para a regulação hídrica da cidade. Já está devidamente documentada na literatura científica a relação positiva entre a biodiversidade e o sequestro de carbono. Assim, restaurar a biodiversidade dessas UCNs pode contribuir significativamente para o sequestro de carbono e para a adaptação da cidade do Recife aos efeitos da crise climática. Em estudo realizado pela equipe da Secretaria de Meio Ambiente e Sustentabilidade, estimou-se um custo de 14 milhões de reais para implementação de uma amplo programa de restauração com a execução das ações previstas nos planos de manejo. É importante ressaltar que essa iniciativa é inovadora. São poucas as cidades que possuem um planejamento para restauração da biodiversidade em seus territórios. Além disso, a iniciativa é inovadora por conta de seu impacto sócio-ambiental. A implementação de um programa de restauração da biodiversidade gerará empregos de um tipo ainda não visto na região: empregos verdes. Em parceria com a comunidade podem ser geradas milhares de empregos diretos e indiretos com uma pegada ambiental reduzida e com potencial de neutralização das emissões.

column19: On April 9, 2020, the City of Phoenix Civic Improvement Corporation (the “Corporation”) issued $290,000,000 Junior Lien Water System Revenue Bonds, Series 2020B (the “Series 2020B Bonds”). The Series 2020B Bonds are designated such based upon the social impacts of sustainable, clean water management as well as the climate adaptation and/or mitigation benefits of the Colorado River Resiliency projects. The Series 2020B Bonds will partially finance the Sustainability Projects. As of May 31, 2025, $286,828,668 of the $290,000,000 bond proceeds Series 2020B Bonds have been spent. The City intends to spend the rest of the Series 2020B bond proceeds in fiscal year 2025-26. The Drought Pipeline is now in service and currently operating to mitigate drought conditions on the Colorado River. The Drought Pipeline Project brings water to north Phoenix to make sure all residents have access to safe, reliable, and clean drinking water during times of shortage on the Colorado River. The project is essential to Phoenix's economic health and vitality, serving up to 400,000 residents. The Water Services Department's construction of the Drought Pipeline was completed in August 2023. The Drought Pipeline interconnects the northern part of the Water System's 543 square mile service area, previously only supplied with Colorado River water, with the southern part of the Water System currently supplied with Salt and Verde River water. The interconnection will ensure the City's ability to provide reliable service to the population in the northern portion of the Water System in the event of reduced availability of Colorado River water, due in part to climate change and the aridification of the Colorado River system basin. The Sustainability Projects has provided new mains, booster pump stations, and pressure-reducing valves that now interconnect the northern and southern transmission and distribution systems so that alternative water supplies can be moved across the entire Water System (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/development-infrastructure/our-infrastructure/drought-pipeline-project.html ). The City is committed to be a leader in sustainability and has established 2050 Environmental Sustainability Goals (“Sustainability Goals”) that articulate the community's desired long-term environmental outcomes that would fulfill the General Plan aspirations of a sustainable desert city. The Sustainability Goals include providing a clean and reliable 100-year supply of water. The Sustainability Goals and other sustainability-related information are available at https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/sustainability.html . The Sustainability Projects are intended to advance the purposes of the Sustainability Goals and to generally comply with the “Green Bond Principles,” “Social Bond Principles” or the “Sustainability Bond Guidelines” promulgated by the International Capital Market Association (“ICMA”) in June 2018. The Series 2020B Bonds will not constitute “exempt facility bonds” issued to finance “qualified green building and sustainable design projects” within the meaning of Section 142(1) of the Code. Impacts from the Sustainability Projects are also aligned with several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (“UN SDGs”). By reference to the ICMA “Green and Social Bonds: A High-Level Mapping to the Sustainable Development Goals” (June 2019), the Sustainability Project primarily aims to address goals 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and 13 (Climate Action). To see the full disclosure, please visit https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/06-30-2024%20Sustainability%20Bonds.pdf?appId=aemshell

Esses espaços são identificados como estratégicos para a implantação do projeto, pois são áreas residuais, já integrantes das ações estratégicas de políticas públicas ambientais do município e com grande potencial para abrigar soluções baseadas na natureza e que representa um passo importante da Prefeitura Municipal de Porto Alegre na construção de uma nova abordagem no manejo de águas pluviais do município. The Project consists of two sites, Chollas Station Road and College Avenue. The existing 24-inch reinforced concrete pipe (RCP)/corrugated metal pipe (CMP) storm drains in the Chollas Station Road site will be replaced and realigned with a 60-inch RCP storm drainpipe system, a new custom designed inlet (located within the North Chollas Community Park), and a concrete energy dissipater with a riprap pad at the outlet. The proposed improvements at the College Avenue site consist of two Modular Wetland Units to treat the 85th percentile stormwater quality runoff from a 15.2 acre fully urbanized area, in addition to ancillary storm drainpipes and laterals in Racine Road. column15: Replacement of sludge treatment and recovery unit
column17: Project partially funded and seeking additional funding
column19: The JR Marcotte waste water plant is the highest municipal GHG emitter on Montreal island. The projet is meant to replace all incinerators within the next ten years by technologies including biomethanization. The project aims to replace the 4 existing multiple hearth incinerators which are a major source of GHG emissions. The alternative to incinerators is to implement 3 technologies: fluidized bed incineration, anaerobic digestion and thermal drying. The sludge from the treatment plant will be treated at 60% by incineration and 40% by anaerobic digestion followed by thermal drying.Anaerobic digestion is a natural biological process of decomposition of sewage sludge by microorganisms which activate under anaerobic conditions, i.e. without oxygen. This process takes place in a closed bioreactor which converts part of the solids in biogas and the remaining solids in digestate. Methane or biogas from this process will be recovered and used to heating the sludge while the surplus will be injected into the natural gas distribution network of a private distributor.Fluidized bed incineration is a proven technology for the high temperature combustion of municipal sludge. The sludge is mixed with a bed of sand which is constantly in motion. This technology is newer than hearth incinerators multiple and operates at higher temperatures. This higher temperature produces less N2O, a powerful GHG that is nearly 300 times greater than the GWP (Global Warming Potential) of CO2. This type of incinerator also makes it possible to reduce the air emissions from existing incinerators. It will also be possible to recover the heat from the hot gases which will be used as an energy source for the production of steam (heating of buildings) and for thermal drying. Thermal drying or thermal stabilization consists in evaporating the water contained in the sludge or in the dehydrated digestates. This process will be powered by heat from fluidized bed incineration and no other external energy input will be required.Phase 1 of the project, the installation and commissioning of an anaerobic digester, will extend from 2024 to 2026. Phase 2, four fluidized bed incinerators and four thermal dryers, will be carried out from 2029 to 2031. And phase 3, four anaerobic digesters, will run from 2031 to 2033. From the point of view of environmental benefits, it is estimated that a reduction of 2,399,970 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over a period of 40 years would be attributable to the project. A grant application to the federal Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program (https://www.infrastructure.gc.ca/plan/icp-pic-INFC-eng.html) has been submitted by the City. This request as been reviewed. Both federal and provincial have conditionally committed to financing a significant portion of the project.

As part of the ecological transition of the Montréal agglomeration, particular attention is being given to the development of sustainable mobility, especially through the enhancement of the cycling network and the interconnection of mobility hubs. This initiative aligns directly with the objectives of the Climate Plan, which aims to reduce reliance on single-occupancy vehicles and promote active and collective modes of transportation.
A government grant has been received to support planning and strategic analysis activities related to this network. This funding enables in-depth studies of current and future needs in active mobility, taking into account territorial dynamics, residential densities, employment hubs, and public transit infrastructure, including REM stations.
The proposed projects include the creation and extension of multifunctional cycling corridors, the redevelopment of strategic areas such as the Canora station surroundings, Saint-Jean Boulevard, and the Île-aux-Tourtes bridge. These interventions aim to improve connectivity between neighborhoods, parks, mobility hubs, and new residential developments, while ensuring universal and safe access.
Special attention is also being given to integrating biodiversity principles and sustainable stormwater management into the design of paths and infrastructure. These elements not only strengthen the resilience of infrastructure to climate change but also enhance the quality of life for residents.
Finally, cross-cutting and pilot projects are being developed to test innovative approaches to mobility, aligned with the specific needs of different territories and the broader GHG reduction goals. These initiatives will help guide future funding applications and structure upcoming interventions within a coherent and sustainable framework.

It is a central funding source for environmental projects that are working to benefit both nature and people. It matches funding from philanthropists, private donors and compensation funds with projects across Greater Manchester.

GMEF can ensure there is funding available for projects working to resolve environmental and natural health issues in the diverse communities around Greater Manchester through funding from donors, enforcement undertakings, and taxes and levies such as landfill tax and carrier bag charges. It has supported over 100 projects across Greater Manchester, ranging from encouraging recycling and reuse to improving green space across the region and creating and restoring habitats.

Singapore hopes to be able to partner more private sector players in developing climate change solutions for Singapore and the world. Promising areas that Singapore has a niche in include clean technology, waste and water technology, urban management and solutions and green ICT. Many global leaders in these fields have chosen to base their R&D and manufacturing operations in Singapore, utilising the talent pool here to grow their operations for the Asia Pacific markets. Such R&D activities are part of an expanding and vibrant cluster in Singapore, and we aim to provide private sector companies with access to a combination of technology, markets, capital and talent.

Under the Research, Innovation, and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 plan, the Urban Sustainability and Solutions (USS) domain will further strengthen our capacities in building Singapore as a liveable, resilient, sustainable and economically vibrant city. We will build on our efforts and increase funding support to 3 areas: (i) understanding, mitigating and adapting to climate change, (ii) developing Singapore as a city that promotes citizens health and well-being through built environment interventions and (iii) transforming our built environment to become more sustainable while optimising our limited manpower and resources.

For (i), USS will adopt a multi-pronged approach to prepare Singapore for the impact of climate change. We will invest in research that deepens our understanding of climate change impact, such as understanding sea-level rise, changing weather patterns, and impact on zoonotic disease transmission. We will develop cost-effective solutions to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions and increase our use of renewables and low carbon technologies such as green/low-carbon materials for the built environment, low-carbon hydrogen and novel carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) technologies. We will also ensure that we are able to adapt and build resiliency to the impact of climate change by developing solutions to address coastal and marine challenges arising from climate change, to protect our coasts, resources and people against sea levels and temperatures. Given Singapore's strategic location in a region of rich biodiversity, there are also opportunities to conserve and leverage our natural assets to meet sustainability goals. This includes developing multi-functional greenery, accelerating industry's adoption of energy efficiency technologies in buildings and exploring nature-based solutions for climate change mitigation and adaptation.

For (ii) and (iii), USS will also leverage modelling and simulation tools to better model environmental factors and the impact on building and infrastructure health and lifespan, and develop effective technologies/materials to strengthen structural integrity of buildings. USS will also continue to tackle heat stress through infrastructure interventions, and deepen our understanding in managing impact of heat and improving community heat resilience.

In Budget 2022, the Singapore Government announced that the public sector will issue up to S$35 billion of public sector green bonds by 2030. This will include bonds issued by the Singapore Government as well as its Statutory Boards.

The Singapore Government published the Singapore Green Bond Framework (Framework) in June 2022, which lays the foundation for the issuance of green bonds by the Singapore Government under the Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act 2021 (SINGA), and serves as a reference for Statutory Boards' respective green bond frameworks.

The Framework is developed and structured in alignment with the core components and key recommendations of the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) Green Bond Principles 2021 and the ASEAN Capital Markets Forum ASEAN Green Bond Standards 2018. The Framework details the Singapore Government's (i) intended use of green bond proceeds, (ii) governance structure to evaluate and select eligible projects, (iii) operational approach to manage green bond proceeds, and (iv) commitment to post-issuance allocation and impact reporting.

Morningstar Sustainalytics, an independent ESG research firm, has completed an external review (Second-Party Opinion) on the green credentials of the Framework, and is of the view that the Framework is credible, impactful and aligns with internationally recognised market principles and standards.

The Singapore Government is updating the Framework to align with the Singapore-Asia Taxonomy, which was released in December 2023.

As at 31 March 2024 (end of Financial Year 2023), the Singapore Government has issued S$5.2 billion sovereign green bonds to finance the expansion of Singapore's electric rail network and green our transportation system.

More information on the Singapore Green Bond Framework and Second-Party Opinion can be found at https://go.gov.sg/greenbonds.'

column19: Objet L'objectif du projet est de proposer des structures types d'éco-organisme capable d'assurer une gestion circulaire des déchets secs en vue d'atteindre le cap de zéro déchet à la décharge. Résultats attendusA travers ce projet l'IECA espère récolter les résultats ci-dessous : •Des cadres types (technique, organisations financières) de mise en œuvre des filières de collecte, de valorisation et/ou de réutilisation des déchets secs sont identifiés •Un cahier des charges type de l'éco-organisme est élaboré•Un programme de renforcement des capacités des acteurs de la gestion des déchets est élaboré•Un programme de sensibilisation des consommateurs est lancé.Description de la situationL'économie circulaire s'inscrit dans un projet de société, dont la mise en œuvre implique la Le territoire du grand Abidjan produit 6000 T de déchets par jour dont 4000 sont collectés et entreposés dans un centre d'enfouissement technique à 41 km du centre-ville. Les déchets secs représentent 16% des déchets produits sur le territoire. La gestion des déchets ménagers est du ressort de l'Agence Nationale de la Gestion de Déchets, qui a octroyé par appel d'offre les marchés à 2 entreprises pour une période qui s'achève en 2025. La tutelle de cette agence fait partie de l'organe de décision de l'Institut de l'Economie Circulaire d'Abidjan (IECA) créé par le District Autonome d'Abidjan. Le conseil d'orientation de l'IECA a jugé prioritaire, la mise en œuvre des actions de valorisation des déchets secs dont la gestion actuelle par le secteur informel pourrait engendrer des sommes importantes pouvant couvrir les charges de collecte et de mise en dépôt actuellement pratiquées. En application du principe de la Responsabilité Elargie du Producteur, et en attribuant à ces déchets secs une valeur marchande, certains pourraient s'autofinancer alors que d'autres auront besoin d'appui financier complémentaire. Il s'impose à l'IECA de solliciter un appui technique et financier à l'effet d'étudier les structurations possibles de gestion des différentes filières.Contraintes liées au projetLa mise en œuvre du programme pourrait être freinée par :La complexité de la mise en œuvre de ce nouveau mode de gestion des déchets secs. La démarche doit se faire par étape. Les déchets pris en compte pour commencer sont les déchets qui ne concernent pas le marché en cours ;La gestion des déchets secs est assurée par une pléthore d'acteurs informels ;Les habitudes socioculturelles de la population peuvent être un obstacle aux performances du modèle ;L'ignorance du tri et la collecte différenciée des déchets. BénéficiairesLe programme bénéficiera Les bénéficiaires du projet sont : la population, le District Autonome d'Abidjan, l'Etat de Côte d'Ivoire, les industriels, les acteurs actuels de la gestion des déchetsCibleLes cibles du projet sont : les commerçants, les industriels, les producteurs de déchets, les consommateurs, les bureaux d'études, les acteurs de la gestion des déchets.

column19:
El Plan Maestro Cali Sostenible es un instrumento integral de política pública diseñado para impulsar la acción medioambiental en la ciudad de Santiago de Cali. Este plan no solo funciona como una herramienta de acción climática local, sino que también posiciona a la ciudad en la lucha global contra el cambio climático.

En cuanto a la mitigación del cambio climático, se estructuró el Plan de Descarbonización de Cali, en el que se identificaron diez macroproyectos con potencial de reducción de Gases de Efecto Invernadero (GEI) en tres sectores estratégicos: transporte, energía y gestión de residuos. Esto permitirá a la ciudad avanzar significativamente en la reducción de emisiones de GEI en tres horizontes temporales: 2030, 2040 y 2050.

En términos generales, se estima que, mediante la implementación de los macroproyectos propuestos, las emisiones de GEI de Cali se reducirán en un 67 % para 2050. El Plan de Descarbonización no solo opera como una hoja de ruta climática local, sino que también posiciona a Cali como un actor clave para el cumplimiento de los compromisos climáticos de Colombia, incluyendo la meta de reducción del 51 % de emisiones para 2030 establecida en la Estrategia de Largo Plazo (E2050), así como el cumplimiento del Acuerdo de París mediante la correcta ejecución de su Contribución Determinada a Nivel Nacional (NDC).

In an effort to address the urban transport problems and also take advantage of the growing densities of population and economic activities in Accra, a Ghana Urban Transport Project was proposed with the following objectives:1.Improve mobility in areas of participating Metropolitan/Municipal/District Assemblies (MMDAs), through a combination of traffic engineering measures, management improvements, regulation of the public transport industry, and implementation of Bus Rapid Transport (BRT) system; and2.Promote a shift to more environmentally-sustainable transport modes and lower transport-related GHG emissions along the pilot BRT corridor in Accra. column19:
Tallinn is seeking financing to support a large-scale residential building renovation initiative aimed at improving energy efficiency and accelerating the city's transition toward climate neutrality. The comprehensive renovations of apartment buildings include upgrades to insulation, windows, heating systems, and ventilation as well as transition from gas, stove, or electric heating to district heating. To accelerate energy-efficient renovation of residential buildings, Tallinn is exploring a value-generating financing model that allows homeowners to fund retrofits by adding new living space. This approach involves:
Constructing an additional floor, annex, or extension to an existing building.
The sale or rental of the newly created units generates revenue.
This revenue is then used to finance the renovation and energy retrofit of the original structure.
This model reduces upfront costs for homeowners or apartment associations and encourages densification in urban areas without new land use.

column17: Project partially funded and seeking additional funding
column19:
Conservation measures for SACs (Special Areas of Conservation) refer to interventions aimed at protecting and maintaining the conservation status of habitats and species within these protected areas. SACs are part of the Natura 2000 network, a European network of protected areas created to ensure biodiversity by conserving natural habitats and species of community interest.

Examples of conservation measures in SACs include:

Habitat management and maintenance: Actions aimed at preserving the natural characteristics of a habitat, such as preventing the spread of invasive species, controlling weeds, or managing grazing areas.

Ecological restoration: Interventions to restore degraded ecosystems, improve soil or water quality, and recreate natural habitats that have been altered or destroyed.

Biodiversity monitoring: Continuous monitoring of species and habitats to assess their conservation status and identify potential problems or threats.

Fauna protection interventions: Projects to protect vulnerable or endangered animal species, such as creating ecological corridors, protecting breeding areas, or regulating human activities.

Control of human activities: Regulating and managing human activities within SACs to reduce the impact on flora and fauna, such as controlling tourism, fishing, or agricultural activities.

The purpose of the Zero Emissions Fleet Transition Plan is to guide MATA's transition into zero emission bus (ZEB) fleet and infrastructure for fixed route service and illustrate how these actions align over time towards a fully zero emissions fleet. The Zero Emissions Fleet Transition Plan is guided by the following set of goals:
• Goal 1: Begin transitioning the first 25 percent of the bus fleet towards a ZEB fleet with efforts currently underway to purchase BEBs that will be charged at the existing bus facility with identified resources. By 2027, there is potential to surpass this goal and reach a transition of 30-40 percent ZEBs in total.
• Goal 2: By 2023, evaluate potential technologies and strategies to transition the remaining 75 percent of the fleet to ZEBs and accommodate those needs at a planned new facility capable of accommodating up to 300 buses in total, operational by 2027. By 2040, there is potential to reach 75 percent ZEB fleet, with a full fleet transition occurring by 2050.
• Goal 3: Use the transition to zero emissions as an opportunity to serve the greater Memphis community and improve their quality of life through reduced emissions and improved air quality.
• Goal 4: Utilize the zero emissions technology that captures the best balance of vehicle and infrastructure reliability, service needs, vehicle cost, infrastructure cost, fuel cost, and fuel availability and reliability.

column19: O Programa Seja Circular, iniciativa do Plano de Ação Climática da cidade, tem como objetivo estimular a adoção dos princípios da Economia Circular e a geração de negócios na área. Os princípios da economia circular incluem a preservação e fortalecimento do capital natural, a otimização do uso dos recursos materiais e a maximização da eficiência do sistema. Os conceitos de economia circular podem ajudar a melhorar a eficiência hídrica e energética e a gestão de resíduos, além de reduzir o desemprego e a informalidade. Com isso, o Programa Seja Circular criará novas oportunidades de geração de renda e redução dos impactos ambientais das cadeias produtivas. O Programa terá como foco comunidades de baixa renda e a assistência a start-ups e negócios existentes para a adoção de princípios de economia circular. Em 2023 foi lançada uma plataforma online que oferece materiais, workshops e seminários sobre os princípios da economia circular. A plataforma online contem informações úteis para aumentar a conscientização sobre modelos circulares e para ajudar as empresas a aplicar os princípios da economia circular e sustentável aos seus produtos, serviços e uso de materiais. O programa ajuda a criar negócios e empregos verdes na cidade, desenvolvendo hackathons de economia circular em bairros de baixa renda e treinando e capacitando a força de trabalho nos princípios da economia circular. Portanto, vai gerar riqueza para as comunidades que ficaram sem renda devido à pandemia COVID-19.Além disso, o programa contribui para o desenvolvimento de uma economia de baixo carbono, reduzindo a geração de resíduos e aumentando o reaproveitamento de materiais na cadeia produtiva. A redução da geração de resíduos também ajudará a diminuir o risco de enchentes e deslizamentos causados pelo descarte inadequado de resíduos em assentamentos informais da cidade. Assim, promoverá a justiça climática e reduzirá a emissão de gases de efeito estufa.

column19: Este proyecto consiste en la modernización, reemplazo y expansión del sistema de alumbrado público del Distrito Metropolitano de Quito (DMQ), reemplazando las luminarias convencionales (alrededor de 223,000) por alumbrado público eficiente, promoviendo la eficiencia energética, la seguridad ciudadana, la reducción de la huella de carbono de la ciudad y generar ahorros para los ciudadanos y el gobierno municipal. Un reemplazo total de las luminarias convencionales podría significar reducir a la mitad (0.5%) la contribución del alumbrado público a la huella de carbono de Quito. El proyecto promueve la seguridad energética, al reducir el consumo de electricidad en el alumbrado público (6% del consumo total de electricidad en la ciudad ; el doble del promedio regional), además, la instalación de lámparas LED, que tienen mejores tasas de eficiencia (conversión de energía en flujo luminoso) que las lámparas convencionales, mejora los niveles de iluminación dentro del espacio público y reduce la contaminación visual y el desperdicio de luz. Debido a su fuerza física y tecnología, las lámparas LED tienen una vida útil mucho mayor (hasta 40 veces) que las lámparas incandescentes convencionales, y pueden reciclarse. El proyecto mejora el acceso a la electricidad, ya que la energía ahorrada se puede distribuir a los usuarios que actualmente no tienen acceso a los servicios de electricidad en hogares, empresas e industrias. Además, un diseño de iluminación adecuado mejora los niveles de luz, aumenta la seguridad y el atractivo estético de la ciudad para los residentes y visitantes. En cooperación con el gobierno nacional, la empresa pública local de electricidad (Empresa Eléctrica de Quito - EEQ) y las partes interesadas privadas, en los últimos años el municipio ha rehabilitado y optimizado el alumbrado público, centrando los esfuerzos en el centro histórico de Quito, donde 2.940 bombillas convencionales tienen ha sido reemplazado por sistemas de iluminación eficientes (LED), con una inversión de US $ 3 millones, lo que implica una reducción en el consumo equivalente a US $ 128,000 por año, lo que representa el desplazamiento de 715,000 tCO2e. El siguiente paso del proyecto es reemplazar el alumbrado público ornamental en Quito, ubicado en parques urbanos y áreas verdes, lo que significa el reemplazo de 1.756 luminarias concentradas principalmente en postes (77%), el suelo (17%) y fachadas (6%) , con un presupuesto de aproximadamente US $ 1 millón. Además, todos los rayos convencionales de Quito serán reemplazados.

column19: Generación de electricidad con el biogás del relleno sanitario de Quito. Este proyecto consiste en la utilización del biogás del relleno sanitario de Quito para la generación de electricidad, como parte de la política de cero residuos del Distrito, que promueve la prevención, minimización y separación de fuentes de residuos, así como una recolección, tratamiento y eliminación de residuos responsable y eficiente. La empresa pública metropolitana de gestión de residuos sólidos (EMGIRS) está a cargo del relleno sanitario de Quito \'El Inga\', donde se depositan los residuos sólidos domésticos recogidos de la ciudad y 33 parroquias rurales desde 2003 (aproximadamente 2.000 toneladas por día, de las cuales el 57% son residuos orgánicos, el 24% son residuos reciclables y el 19% son rechazos). Existe una red de tuberías para capturar biogás dentro de todo el relleno sanitario \'El Inga\', que conduce a una chimenea donde se incinera el biogás. Con una inversión de aproximadamente US $ 7 millones, a fines de 2015 habrá una planta de energía de biogás ensamblado dentro del relleno sanitario “El Inga”, comenzando a generar 2MW / h, y esperando generar 5MW / h para fines de 2016. La generación de energía eléctrica a través del biogás del relleno sanitario de Quito contribuye a la red nacional, como fuente de energías renovables convencionales, apoyando la nueva matriz energética nacional. También mitiga el impacto ambiental causado por la emisión de gases de efecto invernadero, en este caso, metano. Esta acción reducirá 144,000 tCO2e por año.

column19: Este proyecto propone llevar a cabo una gestión completa y adecuada de los residuos líquidos de Quito generados por la población (descargas domésticas) y actividades productivas (descargas industriales), mediante la intercepción, el transporte y el tratamiento de las aguas residuales de la ciudad, descontaminando 246 km de los ríos de Quito y corrientes, minimizando los impactos que actualmente se derivan de descargas directas, mejorando la calidad de vida de la población. La infraestructura consiste en la construcción de tuberías principales de alcantarillado y colectores marginales secundarios, que transportan aguas residuales a las plantas de recuperación de agua. Se instalarán interceptores, haciendo desaparecer los malos olores, mejorando la calidad del aire y la convivencia ciudadana pacífica cerca de los ríos ahora contaminados. Proponer transformar las zonas de influencia degradadas de los ríos en áreas utilizables para riego y energía hidroeléctrica, así como áreas verdes para recreación y paisajismo, correctores ecológicos potenciales para la protección de la biodiversidad. Además, el proyecto propone la generación de electricidad renovable mediante la construcción de tres plantas hidroeléctricas. Además de convertir el proyecto en autosuficiente, la electricidad generada cambiará la venta del exceso de producción (28 MW / h) al sistema de distribución de electricidad de la ciudad o el país. Esto evitará la generación termoeléctrica, lo que generará ahorros económicos al evitar el uso de combustibles fósiles y al mismo tiempo reducirá las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero a la atmósfera. Solo se ha construido una planta de recuperación de agua en el sur de la ciudad, la planta Quitumbe, con Una inversión de 12,5 millones de dólares.

Indianapolis has an outdated solid waste infrastructure and fee system. Indianapolis is without a universal recycling system and has no commercial-scale organics composting providers. 

In early 2024, the Indianapolis Department of Public Works released a series of requests for proposal for the disposal and processing of solid waste for the 279,000 households it services. These processes include traditional trash, diversion of recyclable materials in an improved recycling system, and investigation of the disposal and processing of organic material. As of October 1, 2024, these contracts are being negotiated with selected vendors. 

RFPs for the collection and hauling of these same materials will be released in late 2024. These procurement processes aim to align with Thrive Indianapolis's goals of providing universal residential curbside recycling to all Indianapolis residents and offering subscription curbside composting to all Indianapolis residents. 

Office of Sustainability is assisting DPW in these efforts and assisting in developing grant applications for EPA's Recycling Education and Outreach and Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling grant applications to fund the advancement of this work.

Energy renovation, extension, and construction of public sector buildings for the period until 2030 Programme (City of Zagreb Official Gazette no. 19/22), shorthand as
“EODIZ Programme” defines the activities of preparation and implementation of energy renovation, extension and building construction projects until 2030 and establishes a
permanent and efficient planning structure, investment implementation and building maintenance. The program specifically distinguishes between the period until 2026 with
the aim of using funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (“NPOO”) and the period until 2030, in which alternative procurement models are introduced with the
aim of using funds from the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for the period 2021. - 2027.
The goal of the Program is to implement a large number of projects without raising the level of indebtedness of the City of Zagreb, to establish a systematic and effective
energy renovation, construction, and extension of public sector buildings, while gradually achieving the goal of decarbonization and reduction of operational costs of
operation and maintenance of buildings.
The program is implemented in several phases in order to build the necessary management structure gradually and efficiently and optimally use all available EU, national
and own (budgetary) funding sources. The stages of implementation of the Program include:

As part of this project, a highly innovative, fully automated power-to-methanol (PtM) plant, which is currently located on the campus of the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KlT), for the production of methanol from CO2 from biogas, is to be connected directly to the biogas source of the municipal sewage company. The main aim is to further develop and test the technology under real test conditions. The technology has the potential to contribute significantly to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions and mark a major step towards an energy self-sufficient sewage treatment plant.
By integrating the PtM plant into the Mannheim wastewater treatment plant, it will be possible for the first time to produce methanol as a liquid energy source fully automatically and under dynamic process conditions. The project thus promotes the goal of developing an energy self-sufficient wastewater treatment plant, one of the core objectives of Mannheim's
2030 climate protection action plan.
Power-to-methanol (PtM) is a process for producing methanol by converting CO2 and hydrogen, whereby the hydrogen is obtained from water and renewable electricity using electrolysis.

column19: The large sewage treatment plant of the municipal sewage works is to become energy self-sufficient in the medium term. This means that it will be able to supply itself with electricity and heat. To achieve this, energy saving and energy generation measures were implemented. In addition to the energy renovation of the digester building shell, the heat distribution was optimised, a heat storage tank was built and the sludge drying system was replaced. Most of the required energy is generated by means of an innovative CHP plant, which uses the generated sewage gas to produce electricity and heat. The amount of sewage gas is significantly increased by accepting co-substrates (liquid waste materials containing carbon). In addition, a photovoltaic system was built over water surfaces and the plant's own water wheel.The aim of the measure is to make the sewage treatment plant self-sufficient in terms of energy. The measure is already underway and electricity and heat have been generated on the grounds of the sewage treatment plant for its own use for almost 50 years (Stadt Mannheim, 2010). By 2023, it is planned that so much energy can be generated on the grounds of the sewage treatment plant that it can be operated as energy self-sufficient as possible.The measures already implemented can save 35,000 t of CO2 per year. 26.7 million have already been approved for the energy measures via business plans. A large part of this has already been implemented or is in the process of being implemented. In addition, subsidies are being applied for for the heat storage tank, which will subsidise 30% of the established costs. Further investments depend on the development of the taxation of electricity feed-in. As soon as it is legally and contractually permitted to feed self-generated green energy into the higher-level grid, further energy measures (wind turbine, additional PV systems over water surfaces) are to be included in the business plan. For this further development, the staff position of an energy management will be created.\n\nThe financing of several wind turbines on the site of the sewage treatment plant is not yet clear.

column19: Este proyecto se enmarca dentro del “Plan Maestro para la Regeneración Urbana, Eco-Rehabilitación y Vitalización de los Barrios de Vitoria-Gasteiz” que está desarrollando el Ayuntamiento de Vitoria-Gasteiz de las zonas más desfavorables para el horizonte de veinte años (periodo 2021 - 2040). Cuenta con financiación del Gobierno vasco a través del . Plan interinstitucional de inversiones estratégicas PIIE-24. El proyecto consiste en la regeneración a nivel urbano, social y ambiental del barrio Zaramaga declarado como Área Degradada. Este barrio es predominantemente residencial y la mayoría de los bloques de viviendas fueron construidos entre los años 60 y 70 con sistemas constructivos tradicionales. El proyecto se desarrollará por fase, En la Fase 1 se pretende actuar sobre el 21% de los inmuebles residenciales del Área Degradada (AD) y las calles aledañas, un total de 525 viviendas. El barrio presenta un elevado grado de vulnerabilidad social y/o económica. Las actuaciones planteadas buscan ayudar a la descarbonización de la ciudad y por ello se centran en la rehabilitación con criterios de eficiencia energética de su parque edificado (sobre envolventes + sistemas de calefacción y ACS), tanto público como privado, para lograr un menor consumo energético incorporando recursos de generación sostenibles, la mejora de la accesibilidad, la incorporación de infraestructura verde, el apoyo a una movilidad más sostenible y activa. Se va a impulsar y apoyar a las Comunidades de Vecinos desde la Oficina de Proximidad, como continuación de un programa municipal ya en marcha, para instalar en el barrio 525 kWp (1 kWp/vivienda) de energía solar fotovoltaica: 420 kWp en forma de comunidades de autoconsumo compartido y 105 kWp en Comunidades Energéticas. Además, se pretende instalar 285 kWp adicionales en cubiertas municipales (de colegios y un campo de fútbol) y 35 kWp en una pérgola sobre una zona de juegos infantil, para cesión parcial de energía a las comunidades. Reducción de emisiones de la fase 1 .558 t CO2/año. Generación de energía renovable: 971.750 kWh/año. column19: Like more than 770 communities across the nation, Kansas City is faced with a challenge to meet federal requirements to improve water quality by reducing the frequency and volume of sewer overflows.On September 27, 2010, The United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri entered a consent decree in the case U.S. vs. The City of Kansas City, Missouri (Civil Action No. 4:10-cv-0497-GAF (the “Consent Decree“).Kansas City's Smart Sewer program is a 25-year plan to meet the requirements of the City's Federal Consent Decree. The program represents a $4.5-$5 billion dollar investment-the largest infrastructure investment in Kansas City's history and the first federally approved Consent Decree to incorporate green solutions.The 25-year program outlines a city-wide approach to addressing sewer overflows, improving water quality and supporting local workforce development. Our plan for Kansas City is to fix the City's existing sewer system before investing in new, more costly solutions such as tunnels and storage tanks.Kansas City is committed to leveraging each dollar invested as part of the Smart Sewer program to improve communities and the local workforce. In 2016 Kansas City's Middle Blue River Basin Green Infrastructure project received the prestigious Envision Platinum Award from the Institute for Sustainable Infrastructure. The project is the nation's first Combined Sewer area project to win the award, and is currently the largest integrated green infrastructure project to receive the Envision Platinum Award. The award recognizes the City of Kansas City for exceptional leadership and management of natural resources in the implementation of the green infrastructure project.Also in 2016, Kansas City's Smart Sewer University earned the Kansas City Industrial Council Sustainability Gold Stewardship Award for the program's commitment to local workforce development. OCP University was established in 2013 to assist local MBE, WBE and SLBE business owners in developing the skills and capabilities which are necessary to help firms compete locally and nationally.To date, Smart Sewer University has provided more than 5,300 hours of training to local small, minority and women-owned firms in Kansas City, Missouri.This investment of time and resources has successfully tripled the number of minority firms given the opportunity to serve as the prime contractor by expanding the capacity and capabilities of local firms.On February 21, 2017 the City of Kansas City, Missouri presented the annual Smart Infrastructure Update (program book | presentation) to provide local contractors with information about Fiscal Year 2018 capital improvements projects and capital improvements plans for the next five and ten years of investments as part of the City's Overflow Control Program.Kansas City's wastewater challenges are not unique. In fact, the investment we are making as part of the Overflow Control Program is in direct response to the EPA's federally mandated requirement to improve water quality by reducing wastewater overflows. Kansas City's Smart Sewer program is currently in year seven of a 25-year plan to reduce sewer overflows.

column19: Root Nashville is a public-private campaign, with leadership from Mayoral administrations, to plant 500,000 trees in Davidson County by 2050. The campaign aims to increase the county's tree canopy and create a more equitable distribution of the health and sustainability benefits of trees across all neighborhoods. Davidson County's urban tree canopy is a public utility that improves air quality, manages stormwater, supports public health, and improves quality of life for Nashville residents. In 2016, Metro Nashville convened the Livable Nashville Committee, a group of local public and private leaders, to develop a vision to enhance Nashville's livability and environmental quality. The committee found that, between 2008 and 2016, the tree canopy in Nashville's urban zone had fallen from 28% to 24% (a loss of approximately 9,000 mature trees per year during this timeframe)---far below many comparable cities across the country. In response to the county's rapid development and loss of trees, the Mayor's Livable Nashville Committee proposed a tree-planting campaign to restore the city's urban canopy. Root Nashville has identified five priority outcomes for the campaign that address public health, environmental quality and equity. These priority outcomes will help select neighborhoods to prioritize in planting. •Creating a more equitable distribution of trees throughout the county •Helping mitigate the impacts of respiratory illness such as pediatric asthma •Reducing high heat areas within the city •Improving water quality and reducing stormwater runoff. More information: https://rootnashville.org/•Minimizing the impact of the Emerald Ash Borer on Nashville's tree canopy Community Outreach, Education and Research In addition to planting 500,000 trees, Root Nashville will: •Raise awareness for the campaign and the social, economic and environmental impact of trees •Engage the community through tree celebrations, volunteer planting events, in-school participation and educational workshops •Invest in tree tracking, watering and ongoing maintenance •Collect data on environmental and public health benefits of trees across Nashville

column19: The project aims to undertake a feasibility study on how to harness the collective potential of small-scale embedded generation in the City to form a photovoltaic (PV) project in the City of Tshwane. The aim is to develop a strategy that can guide the City on how to become energy secure by scaling up the use of PV systems The strategy would be based on a model, which will have to be accompanied by a set of mechanisms that aim to enable end-users to invest in solar PV system solutions, engage financial institutions and investors, and attract technology providers. Also, the role of the municipality will be key to orchestrate the strategy and create trust among the different key actors. The strategy will take into account the current policy framework, the resources limitation and the current capacity and infrastructure of the municipal authorities. The strategy will also take into consideration the more suitable sale/financing models that can address the needs of the different market segments. The first step to define a strategy is to select a suitable sale/financing model according to the different market segments (geographic, demographic and income divisions within the city); once the model has been selected it will define the mechanisms that support the models. The prefeasibility study has identified the different financing models to be utilized to scale up in the implementation of the installation if PV Solar system in CoT. The models are presented in a brief description and indication of the role of the most relevant actors is given. An in-depth analysis is needed to select the most appropriate model. The models presented have been successfully tested in a number of countries and can be grouped into two categories: “Sales Models” (which includes cash sales; independent power producer; credit sale and micro finance combine ) , where the end-user (in this case households) is the investor (purchaser) and hence owner of the system; and “Service Models” ( which includes rending ; power purchase agreement and pay as you go ), where the system is owned by a third party which provides the electricity service to the household. It will be possible, or even necessary in some circumstances, to decide on a combination of models within or across the “Service and Sales Model” groups. The choice of model or combination of models will affect the roles and responsibilities of the main actors.Once the suitable models have been selected, actors would need to be identified who can provide the financial services, the technology products, and other complementary services. Also, it would be important to define the technical implications for the municipality to establish a net metering system, define the warranties and commitments of the TSP for the municipality and for the clients (households). The study must define a more appropriate payment system according to the model selected and identify available risk mitigation instruments that can be used to cover a potential financial support from the financial institutions (such as a public guarantee or an insurance). Additionally, a more in-depth analysis should include a list of potential providers (if needed) of solar PV systems and a small evaluation of their position to support the City of Tshwane in their Solar PV system programme.The project has a potential of creating green jobs and reducing carbon emissions. Though the upfront cost may seem to be high, ultimately there will be extensive cost saving to the consumer and the city in the long run.

column19: City of Tshwane has undertaken a study to pilot the integration of the waste pickers into the waste value chain.City of Tshwane is in a critical stage whereby it has to enhance its waste minimization measures in order to improve on the waste management program. City of Tshwane 's transition to a Green Economy will challenge the established economic system that is based on increasing the exploitation of natural resource to fulfil the growing demands for material consumption. Innovation and green technology will play a key role in decoupling material growth from natural resource depletion and in the growth in green jobs. It is unavoidable that all recyclables will not be captured at source, therefore the opportunity for landfill waste picking will remain. The situation on landfills is most often chaotic, without any organized waste picking systems in place. The current system used for waste picking from landfills poses health and safety risks to landfill waste pickers. The only sources of recyclable materials currently accessible to waste pickers, before being transported in RELs where it is compressed and contaminated even further, are those from unsecured residential, commercial, and industrial areas. The systems currently used for waste picking in streets are often considered to result in environmental nuisances like scattered non-recyclable waste, windblown litter, water pollution and air pollution where some wastes are burnt. It also poses high safety risks to the waste pickers when pulling their trolleys along busy roads. The generator/collector of recyclable material is to earn an income from the material that is mostly sold to buyback centers varying in size and services offered.A business model has been developed with various options. A situational analysis was completed which found that there are various sources of the recyclables that have market value. As such, the study recommended four business models to be applied depending on the source of the recyclables. The current economic status of the city requires an innovative way of encouraging recycling and creating an enabling environment for various role players in the waste value chain. Waste pickers are found to be one of the key role-players in the value chain. The city now wants to pilot the model in a small area before it be scaled up. It is important for the city to have a cost benefit analysis of each model and demonstrate the practicalities thereof. The study has shown the fact that for each model to be applied, there are several interrelated factors that need to be taken into consideration. In this case, the city needs to be working closely with the formal and informal waste pickers as the key partners in the programme together with other spheres of government.

The #FreetownTheTreetown campaign is planting, growing, and digitally tracking 1 million trees, restoring 5,000 hectares of land. The approach harnesses innovative, low-cost digital technology for tree-tracking, while creating jobs for women/youth as alternatives to employment in environment-damaging industries such as stone and sand mining and charcoal production. 

#FreetownTheTreeTown is a portfolio of community urban reforestation projects implemented in partnership with a network of community-based organizations (CBOs), where city residents are paid to plant, nurture, digitally track and monitor trees and mangroves throughout the city. Infrastructure Investment Platform, growers are paid for their contribution, and the tree is placed on a public map/geotagged so its survival can be monitored digitally. 

Here is how it works:
●	Step 1: Seedlings supplied to the planting area. Note: Nursery partners commercial and community are selected from within the Western Area (as the project wants to create a targeted green economy effect). 
●	Step 2: Seedlings received by the CBO. Note: There is a way bill signed by the nursery supply partner and the CBO and a digital supply form filled and uploaded to a database by the CBO. The #TreeTown Data Team will import the supply data into the platform.
●	Step 3: CBO allocates planting area and specific number of seedlings to each Grower (minimum 1,000 trees per / Grower with a maximum of 2000 per / Grower) 
●	Step 4: The Growers' will physically tag each seedling. The tag will be an alpha-numeric code provided by the #TreeTown Data Team to each CBO and will be applied as a note upon tracking each tree. The tag will become the digital tree ID number for that individual tree in the platform. 
●	Step 5: Seedlings are distributed to a grower.
●	Step 6: Grower plant the seedling in reforestation areas allocated to the CBO.
●	Step 7: Growers create a Tree Tracker app account on locally available smartphones—including a photo (of the grower).
●	Step 8: Growers use a Tree Tracker app to create a unique geotagged record, or ID, for each new tree planted—including a photo (of the tree). 
●	Step 9: Growers upload the trees planted into the tree tracker platform.
●	Step 10: Trees tracked and uploaded to the platform are verified by tree verification monitors and impact token ID is created. 
●	Step 11: Growers receive mobile money micropayments on the bases of tracked and verified trees allocated to them.
●	Step 12: Growers revisit each verified trees periodically, to water and maintain, verify and document the plant's survival.

As well as increasing urban green areas in Freetown, wide-scale tree planting provides shade in heat waves and protects the city against landslides and flooding. The program is sustained and scaled through the sale of “impact tokens” to institutions, corporations and investors, financing and incentivizing reforestation into the future. column17: Project partially funded and seeking additional funding
column19: In 2023, Mannheim and Freetown began to develop a clean cooking project as part of the Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) Green Citizen Energy programme. They are supported by a consulting services company specializing in carbon offset projects that meet the requirements for certification according to the internationally recognized Gold Standard. The cities have the aim of certifying the project on the voluntary carbon market and eventually financing the implementation of the project through private investors. The result of the joint work was a positive feasibility study for a CO2 compensation project on the subject of clean cooking, which is to be certified according to the Gold Standard. The City of Mannheim's overarching goal is to work towards attracting local companies as investors and thus integrating them into its own development policy commitment. At the same time, Mannheim aims to support the City of Freetown in implementing its own climate protection action plan. Before approaching the private sector, however, a pilot project is to be carried out in order to test the project idea in practice so that costs can be better calculated, implementation and monitoring can be concretized and the acceptance of the more efficient cookstoves and alternative fuel sources by the target group can be tested in practice.

Maintaining and strengthening carbon sinks is a central measure to actively advance, bearing in mind the city's target of being climate positive already from 2029 onwards. column15: Large Scale Retrofitting of Krakow Buildings
column17: Project not funded and seeking full funding
column19:
Project NEEST - NetZero Emission and Environmentally Sustainable TerritoriesBuildings (stationary energy) are the main source of greenhouse gas emissions in cities (about 85% of all emissions without industry). Although the mayor does not have direct competence to decide on private buildings, their inclusion is a prerequisite for the decarbonisation of the city. Five Polish cities are doing project because they have similar challenges that require support from the national level. Cooperation between local governments and the government gives an opportunity to remove barriers and develop effective support programs. Poland, due to the structure of the energy sector, has a long way to go to climate neutrality. Close interaction and rapid learning give you the chance to shorten this distance.As part of the pilot project, we have planned multi-sectoral activities, involving many partners, so that at the same time we want to solve the problems related to urban development.Levers of change in the Large Scale Retrofitting:Change levers are places in a complex system where a small correction leads to a big change in the whole system. These can be technologies, regulations and management methods,financial and business solutions, social innovation, organizational capacity. The following shift levers have been identified:-cooperation of local governments with the government on the preparation of support programs,-model of management and visualization of greenhouse gas emission reduction,-wide availability of best technical solutions and knowledge of good practices,-financing models and business models for building renovations on a massive scale,-the concept of low- or zero-emission district heating,-the concept of an energy-positive district,-organizational and economic model of energy communities,-a model of space management to change transport habits and increase the comfort of life,-social innovations strengthening participation in democratic decision-making;-social innovations that build awareness and change behaviors based on collected and analyzed data,-a platform for cooperation and knowledge sharing with other cities based on the experience and knowledge gained by pilot cities,-Procedure for managing a multi-sectoral, multi-stakeholder portfolio of programs, projects and tasks based on the collected and analyzed data.As to the total cost of project and total investment cost needed, it is not that simple to point. On one hand Krakow has almost 4000 buildings, typical blocks from communism era. Most of them, maybe even all, need deep retrofitting. With average estimated cost of two millions PLN per building, it gives the cost of circa 8 billions PLN, that is 1,7 billion EUR. On the other hand, project like that is very easy to scale, or to divide into smaller projects. For example realization of deep retrofitting for 50 buildings gives the cost of circa 100 million PLN.

Biciclando is a program that promotes recycling and active mobility with a gender perspective. Operated by the 'Bicicladoras,' women specialists in managing recyclable and valuable waste, the initiative provides home collection services using electric-assist bicycles adapted for carrying recycling loads. This program won the Bloomberg Philanthropies' 2021 Global Mayors Challenge, which supports its implementation.

The program has three elements:

Circular Economy Center (CEC):
The CEC focuses on minimizing waste by recycling, reusing, and repurposing materials. It offers workshops and programs to encourage the community and businesses to adopt circular economy principles, transforming waste into valuable resources like compost and upcycled products. This facility serves as the operational base for Biciclando.

Recycling Collection:
This component establishes a system for collecting, sorting, and processing recyclable materials such as PET, paper, aluminum, and TetraPak. It includes curbside pickup, drop-off points, and outreach to local recycling businesses to reduce landfill waste and reintegrate materials into the production cycle.

Cycling Infrastructure:
The cycling infrastructure connects the service area of Biciclando with main streets, featuring dedicated bike lanes and improved safety measures. This promotes bicycle use for commuting and recreation, reducing carbon emissions and enhancing public health.

Funds are required for a second phase.

The municipality of Hermosillo faces a water deficit of approximately 600 liters per second between the available supply and the growing demand for human consumption. Current water sources rely heavily on aquifer recharge through rainfall, and insufficient rainfall, as has been the case, results in service shortfalls, hindering economic diversification and competitiveness due to limited water resources.

To address this, efforts are focused on improving efficiency through the use of renewable energy, fostering a local energy market that supports the energy transition, reduces reliance on fossil fuels, diversifies water sources, and ensures the sustainability of water supply to local communities—ultimately enhancing municipal services.

A feasibility study will assess the potential for desalination of brackish water to provide potable water to Hermosillo's population. The plan includes powering these desalination facilities with solar energy. The project proposes utilizing brackish water from the Sahuaral area, which is currently under a water extraction ban for agriculture due to saline intrusion from the Sea of Cortez. The initiative envisions building infrastructure for water distribution and a desalination plant to boost water supply for human consumption, as well as industrial and agricultural purposes.

column15: Remediación de Laguna del Parque Sarmiento - Ciudad de Córdoba con Nanoburbujas de Ozono (O3)\n
column17: Project not funded and seeking full funding
column18: Public-private partnership|Public finance- national government|Grants|Private investment
column19:
La laguna del Parque Sarmiento presenta un problema de eutrofización, generado por dos fuentes principales: una interna, vinculada a la proliferación de algas por exceso de nutrientes (fósforo y nitrógeno), que produce aguas verdosas, malos olores, disminución de oxígeno disuelto y presencia de toxinas; y una externa, asociada al ingreso constante de agua proveniente de perforaciones con altas concentraciones de nutrientes, lo que actúa como un aporte permanente de contaminación.
Ante este diagnóstico, se propone un Plan de Acción Integrado que combine el tratamiento de la fuente externa (perforaciones) y del problema interno (agua de la laguna). La estrategia contempla: caracterizar las perforaciones, instalar un sistema piloto de filtrado o humedal en una de ellas (dejando la otra como testigo), y aplicar la tecnología de nanoburbujas de ozono en un área delimitada de la laguna (100-200 m²). El plan incluye monitoreo conjunto de calidad del agua y análisis de la sinergia entre ambos tratamientos, con el objetivo de demostrar un modelo circular y sostenible de remediación: reducir el ingreso de nutrientes y regenerar el ecosistema acuático.
Las Nanoburbujas de Ozono (NBs) constituyen una tecnología innovadora: son burbujas ultrafinas (<200 nm) con alta estabilidad y eficiencia de transferencia de gas (85%). El ozono inyectado oxida algas, cianobacterias, patógenos y compuestos orgánicos responsables de olores, y al descomponerse se convierte en oxígeno disuelto, revitalizando el agua sin residuos químicos nocivos.
Frente a métodos tradicionales como alguicidas, aeración mecánica o dragado, las nanoburbujas presentan ventajas: son ecológicas, al generar únicamente oxígeno como residuo; eficientes, por su permanencia en la columna de agua; y seguras, ya que no afectan la flora, fauna ni los usos recreativos de la laguna.
El alcance del servicio piloto contempla 30 días de tratamiento, con posibilidad de extensión a 60 días, sobre un área representativa de la laguna. Los objetivos esperados son: eliminación de algas y cianobacterias, reducción de olores, aumento de oxígeno disuelto, mejora en la transparencia del agua, disminución de carga orgánica y patógenos, junto con un monitoreo constante y reportes técnicos que validen los resultados.

El valor de la prueba piloto es de US$17.700,00 +IVA. El costo total del proyecto si funciona la prueba piloto es de 150.000 US$

column19: Se propone la instalación de una red de monitoreo continuo de variables meteorológicas y de calidad de aire, integrada al sistema de alumbrado público inteligente. Se trata de la incorporación de 50 sensores para la medición sistemática, contínua y permanente de niveles de contaminantes del aire (monóxido de carbono (CO), óxidos de nitrógeno (NO2, NOx), material particulado de 10 y 2.5 micrones ( PM10, PM2,5), ozono (O3), compuestos orgánicos volátiles (COV's) y dióxido de azufre (SO2). Radiaciones No Ionizantes (RNI) y niveles de presión sonora) y variables meteorológicas (temperatura, presión, humedad, velocidad y dirección del viento). Los sensores se instalarán utilizando como soporte físico las columnas del alumbrado público y como soporte de gestión de la información la red de telegestión inteligente del mismo, lo que permitirá un alcance territorial del monitoreo de variables ambientales que cubriría los diferentes sectores de la ciudad. Los datos generados serán publicados para el libre acceso a la comunidad a través del Sistema de Datos abiertos de la ciudad y difundidos a través de diferentes medios en formato de un índice que facilite su interpretación. Asimismo, esta información es clave para el diseño de políticas de protección de la salud pública, prevención de la contaminación ambiental y devastación de ecosistemas vitales, como es el humedal del Delta del Paraná, y será integrada a la gestión de Smart City del Municipio, centralizada en el Centro Integrado de Operaciones de la Municipalidad de Rosario (CIOR). Esta propuesta se encuentran enmarcadas tanto en lo establecido en las líneas estratégicas del Plan Ambiental Rosario -PAR-, en referencia a la contaminación del aire, como en el PLAC, en el eje de Salud, que entre sus directrices sectoriales plantea el mejoramiento de la vigilancia de la calidad del aire.Asimismo, este proyecto dará cumplimiento a las siguientes normativas: Decreto No 58.824, del 20 de agosto de 2020 y de la Ordenanza Municipal No 10.073, del 1 de septiembre de 2020 (modifica el art. 5 de la Ordenanza Municipal No 5820/1994).Cabe señalar que, el desarrollo y la gestión del sistema será implementado mediante procesos de participación y co-creación con actores de la ciudad que vienen trabajando en la temática climática y de calidad de aire en el marco de la gobernanza climática. Entre los objetivos que prevé esta intervención se encuentran: Avanzar en la acción climática mediante la generación de información ambiental de calidad, de manera integrada a la eficiencia y resiliencia del sistema de alumbrado público. Aumentar la cantidad disponible de datos sobre calidad de aire para la toma de decisiones y la información a la población, incrementando el alcance territorial y la cantidad de variables. Establecer procesos de co-creación y colaboración extrema con actores locales para el monitoreo ambiental local en el marco de la gobernanza climática .

El proyecto incluye la construcción de una playa de recepción donde la fracción orgánica es cargada en los biodigestores (recintos con cerramiento hermético) mediante pala frontal. Allí se procede a la inoculación bacteriana mediante una corriente líquida que percola por la masa de residuos, y es recirculada. El biogás generado alimenta una turbina para generación de energía eléctrica que abastecerá el Centro Ambiental donde estará emplazada la planta, reemplazando con energía limpia, la energía eléctrica generada a partir de fuentes fósiles.

column19: Se proyecta la instalación de la primera planta solar fotovoltaica urbana colaborativa en la ciudad de Rosario, localizada en un mercado de productos locales que alberga 40 locales comerciales de pequeñas y medianas empresas, en una de las zonas más transitadas de la ciudad. Con una potencia instalada de 552 kWp tiene como objetivo establecer una experiencia de generación distribuida colaborativa articulando a actores privados y públicos.Las instalaciones ocuparán la cubierta del Mercado del Patio que cuenta con una superficie de 3260 m2 con una orientación adecuada para la captación de energía solar mediante paneles fotovoltaicos, con una capacidad de generación de energía eléctrica aproximada de 864.600 kWh/año, aprovechando los índices de radiación solar de nuestra región. La energía generada, será utilizada por los locales y espacios comunes del Mercado, y el excedente será inyectado a la red, bajo la figura de “prosumidor colaborativo” contemplado en la normativa vigente contribuyendo al reemplazo de consumos del municipio en otros edificios de la administración local.. En la provincia de Santa Fe la modalidad de generación distribuida colaborativa está reglamentada por la Resolución Provincial 316 del 2021. Los comercios y el Municipio pueden participar como Usuarios-Generadores colaborativos asociados, y a partir de una única instalación abastecerse en función de su cuota-parte de participación, utilizando la energía generada para abastecer consumos en el Mercado o en otra ubicación. Finalmente se espera generar una experiencia concreta de implementación de la generación colaborativa y articulación público-privada que pueda identificar modelos de asociación, difundirse e impulsar otras experiencias en la ciudad. De esta manera se reemplazará el consumo de energía eléctrica de origen principalmente fósil (actualmente provista por el sistema interconectado nacional) por energía renovable, permitiendo reducir emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI) y contribuir a las metas climáticas de la ciudad presentes en el Plan Local de Acción Climática. .El proyecto contribuirá a la difusión de este tipo de tecnologías, ya que las instalaciones estarán a la vista del público y en uno de los sectores más transitados de la ciudad, colaborando a mejorar la percepción de la ciudadanía en general, en cuanto a la posibilidad de lograr una transición a energías renovables y crear conciencia e inspirar en los beneficios y factibilidad de implementar este tipo de proyectos. Se estima que la ejecución del proyecto puede reducir la emisión de 236,91 ton.eq CO2 por año, por reemplazo de energía eléctrica de fuentes principalmente fósiles, por energía renovable.La población a beneficiarse implica a todos los habitantes de Rosario ya que se reduce la huella de carbono de la ciudad (1.001.406 habitantes). De manera más directa se beneficia a 200 personas que trabajan en el Mercado y 600 personas que trabajan de manera indirecta. También a quienes visitan el Mercado, que se estima son cerca de un millón de personas al año.

El Programa de Buenas Prácticas Ambientales (BPA) es una herramienta clave para la promoción de la gestión ambiental en emprendimientos y organizaciones en la gestión de recursos, la eficiencia energética y la reducción de impactos ambientales. 

A partir de la elaboración y puesta en marcha del Plan Local de Acción Climática a 2030, y de sus Sistema de Monitoreo, BPA pasó a formar parte de las 62 medidas priorizadas.

En este marco, el BPA implementa nuevas herramientas y recursos técnicos para incorporar un enfoque específico en cuanto a la acción climática, incluyendo diagnósticos como huellas de carbono y evaluaciones de riesgo climático. 

El objetivo es que todas las pequeñas y medianss empresas (PyMes) y todas las instituciones de la ciudad, cuenten con planes de acción que les permitan hacer frente a los desafíos que enfrentamos, como olas de calor, tormentas severas y otros fenómenos meteorológicos extremos, pero también a las oportunidades que esta crisis climática representa. 

En ese marco, estamos en búsqueda de financiamiento para acompañar a empresas e instituciones privadas en la implementación de sus planes de acción climática, elaborados en el marco del programa de Buenas Prácticas Ambientales (BPA). Para facilitar su transición, diseñamos un sistema de préstamos a baja tasa y con plazos de pago amplios. Nuestro objetivo es capitalizar este fondo para asegurar su sustentabilidad en el tiempo y así garantizar la continuidad de la implementación del proyecto.
Por los montos a buscar puede ser variable.
