Sistemas Urbanos de drenaje pluvial

Se analiza la implementación Sistemas Urbanos de Drenaje Pluvial Sostenible, como Jardines de lluvia, Jardín microcuenca, Pavimentos permeables y Zanjas de bioretención, en los cuales se usan plantas y diferentes sustratos para filtrar el agua y como una alternativa a las zanjas y pozos que se usan actualmente, y que desalojan las aguas pluviales junto con grasas, aceites, residuos sólidos y orgánicos que se encuentran en las calles, directamente al subsuelo, y sin ningún método de filtración.
Ya se cuenta con proyectos pilotos, que constan de 4 sistemas: Jardines de lluvia, Jardín microcuenca, Pavimentos permeables y Zanjas de bioretención, en los cuales se usan plantas y diferentes sustratos para filtrar el agua. Este estudio y proyecto parte del tema que, aunque en Mérida hay suficiente agua, no se está cuidado su calidad de manera adecuada y para mejorarla una alternativa es mejorar los sistemas de drenaje. Con este estudio buscamos dos cosas: un sistema de drenaje eficiente, es decir, desalojar el agua de las calles con rapidez y reducir la contaminación del manto acuífero; para tratar de atender estas dos variables vimos que hay sistemas que reproducen el ciclo de la naturaleza y uno ellos son los sistemas de drenaje sustentable.

A Região Urbana do Imbirussu apresenta um problema histórico com alagamentos das vias urbanas. Isso acontece em função de suas características físicas, como a baixa declividade do terreno, solos com baixa capacidade de infiltração e lençol freático aflorante, que não favorecem a absorção da água pelo solo. Além disso, devido ao processo de urbanização e o aumento da intensidade e frequência das chuvas, o volume excedente da água que não é absorvida pelo solo e escoa superficialmente tem sido cada vez maior, sobrecarregando assim o sistema de drenagem urbana. Como consequência as vias públicas se transformaram em canais e depósitos de acúmulo de águas pluviais, que acabam invadindo as residências e prédios comerciais, causando prejuízos materiais e problemas sanitários. 
Neste sentido, o Poder Público Municipal deu início ao desenvolvimento de um projeto com o objetivo de reduzir os alagamentos da referida Região e de incorporar áreas verdes na paisagem urbana. O projeto, denominado Parque dos Ipês, propõe a implantação de uma lagoa que possibilitará um sistema de captação e retardamento do escoamento das águas pluviais; equipamentos de lazer, contemplação, esportes, cultura e para o desenvolvimento de atividades gastronômicas localizado no bairro Santo Antônio. Além disso, irá implantar elementos de drenagem sustentável, como jardins de chuva e canteiros pluviais, em seis bairros, que compõe a referida Região Urbana, a saber: Caiçara, Santo Amaro, Santo Antônio, Sobrinho, Taveirópolis e União; visando complementar as estruturas convencionais de drenagem, e controlar e redirecionar o escoamento das águas pluviais acumuladas nas vias. Serão implementadas aproximadamente 30 Soluções Baseadas na Natureza - SBNs (jardins de chuva e canteiros pluviais) em toda a Região Urbana, além de um Parque Multifuncional em uma área de 12ha. 
Os benefícios contemplarão um valor significativo de pessoas em situação vulnerável, tendo em vista que a microbacia abrange 6 bairros, aproximadamente 70 mil pessoas; das quais, em torno de 11 mil estão em situação de pobreza, sendo mais de 3.583 beneficiários do Bolsa Família e 1.764 idosos com Benefício de Prestação Continuada (Planurb, 2023); ainda, impactará diretamente em 3.562 pessoas, das quais 51,5% são mulheres e 223 pessoas em situação de pobreza (raio de 300m - WRI Brasil 2023); além de 2941 estudantes do ensino infantil ao superior (raio de 500m - Planurb, 2023). Por fim, aproximadamente 1650 negócios são potencialmente impactados nos eventos de precipitação intensa (Planurb, 2023).
O Parque dos Ipês tem o propósito de gerar valor ambiental, econômico e social. Irá promover a adaptação da cidade às mudanças climáticas; redução e resiliência a alagamentos pelo aumento das áreas verdes e implementação de infraestrutura verde e azul. É esperado uma redução do custo com danos materiais e com limpeza após eventos de precipitação intensa; redução do custo com indenizações pagas pela prefeitura após eventos de precipitação intensa; custo evitado com obras de prevenção; redução da frequência de alagamentos e redução das vias urbanas alagadas.
O projeto irá promover a melhora do microclima, na qualidade de vida e no bem-estar e saúde. Isso se dará pela implementação de espaços para interações sociais, com a natureza e práticas esportivas; implementação de áreas verdes na área urbana; aumento da arborização urbana e implementação de espaços para práticas educativas. Após a implementação do projeto espera-se que haja uma redução da temperatura do ar, aumento do índice de qualidade do ar, redução do nível de ruídos por unidade de área de vegetação, aumento da frequência de eventos educativos na região, redução dos custos de hospitalização com doenças respiratórias e causadas por veiculação hídrica e redução custos municipais com ações preventivas a essas doenças.

A Unidade Técnica de Agricultura Urbana foi criada em 26 de agosto de 2021 com o objetivo de promover a segurança alimentar, o desenvolvimento local sustentável e a inclusão social através da agricultura urbana, em conformidade com os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável. A presente proposta visa aprimorar a infraestrutura da Unidade Técnica de Agricultura Urbana (UTA), estabelecida em 26 de agosto de 2021, para fortalecer sua capacidade de cumprir a missão de gestão das Hortas Urbanas de Campo Grande. A reforma e ampliação da sede administrativa, bem como a melhoria das áreas operacionais e a criação de uma horta educativa, são essenciais para otimizar as ações de combate à insegurança alimentar, gerar trabalho e renda, e promover o desenvolvimento local sustentável.
Este projeto visa transformar a UTA em um polo de inovação e difusão do conhecimento, alinhado aos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS). As melhorias incluem:
Reforma da Sede Administrativa: Modernização das instalações para garantir um ambiente de trabalho mais eficiente e acolhedor para a equipe.
Reforma da Área de Manipulação de Alimentos: Adequação do espaço de seleção e manipulação de alimentos, com a instalação de pias e bancadas que atendam às normas de higiene e segurança, facilitando o trabalho e a distribuição dos produtos.
Reforma dos Banheiros: Modernização dos banheiros, garantindo maior conforto e acessibilidade para funcionários e visitantes.
Implementação da Horta Educativa: Criação de um espaço de aprendizado prático para a comunidade, onde serão realizadas oficinas, palestras, cursos e outras atividades educativas sobre técnicas de cultivo e sustentabilidade.

column19: Implantação/Ampliação e monitoramento de projetos-piloto a serem executados na região costeira, visando a diminuição dos prejuízos causados quando há invasão da água do mar junto à infraestrutura urbana existente no local, tal como avenidas, farol, passarelas, além de casas e comércios, constituem-se em uma alternativa viável a curto prazo. Estas obras têm por objetivo também colaborar para ampliar o conhecimento sobre os impactos nas áreas adjacentes e indicar intervenções definitivas para as regiões mais afetadas e/ou de interesse. Métodos tradicionais de proteção costeira tem se mostrado uma opção cara e de difícil manutenção, dado a escassez de rochas naturais. As clássicas estruturas de concreto estão sendo substituídas por materiais mais baratos como geossintéticos, estruturas de gabião, entre outros. Os tubos flexíveis de geotêxtil têm sido aplicados para a construção de diques e quebra-mares em vários projetos ao redor do mundo. Algumas de suas maiores vantagens se constituem no fato de que podem ser preenchidos com materiais encontrados in situ por meio de bombeamento hidráulico, como material de dragagem, além de permitirem uma construção mais rápida e barata que outras tecnologias. Sendo assim, a solução piloto proposta para esta região consiste em um molhe parcialmente submerso construído com geotubos preenchidos com areia da praia, de forma a:- Reduzir o custo de implantação de uma solução definitiva, bem como o risco desta solução ter baixa eficácia e / ou produzir impactos indesejados em regiões adjacentes. Esta consideração se torna especialmente relevante nesta região, em função dos modelos matemáticos aplicados não terem se mostrado capazes de reproduzir as condições locais- Causar o mínimo impacto visual, visto que a área tem atrativo turístico;- Permitir a execução da obra em um curto período de tempo, visto que as dimensões são reduzidas e os métodos construtivos são ágeis;- Permitir uma fácil desmobilização da obra e a inexistência de impactos ambientais decorrentes de sua retirada, caso esta se mostre ineficiente. A estrutura planejada, pode ser removida apenas abrindo os geotubos e os deslocando, de forma a permitir que a areia, que é proveniente da própria praia, saia dos geotubos e sejam recapturadas pelo transporte costeiro, tal como já acontece com a alimentação artificial da praia realizada pela Prefeitura. Atualmente encontra-se na etapa de monitoramento de resultados para análise da pertinência de sua ampliação. A Autoridade do Porto de Santos (APS) contratou a UNICAMP para realizar estudos sobre a erosão costeira e impactos relacionados à dragagem de aprofundamento do canal do estuário (http://www.sindaport.com.br/conteudo-pesquisa.php?id=28314)

column19: No âmbito do Acordo de Cooperação entre a Universidade Santa Cecília (UNISANTA) e a Prefeitura Municipal de Santos, estima-se que entre os anos de 2017 e 2022, foram emitidos aproximadamente 1.765 boletins diários de previsão meteoceanográfica e 108 boletins extraordinários de alertas antecipados de ressacas para a cidade de Santos contabilizados até junho de 2022. Estes alertas são amplamente divulgados pela mídia local, publicados no diário oficial de Santos e disponibilizados no portal web da Prefeitura de Santos, onde é possível encontrar dezenas de notícias relacionadas ao sistema de alerta desenvolvido pela UNISANTA, denotando sua importância para a segurança da cidade.Considerando a qualidade e histórico de aplicação da plataforma pelo município para minimizar os impactos dos eventos marítimos extremos cada vez mais frequentes no meio urbano em atendimento à população vulnerável, e que o acompanhamento e a previsão antecipada dos eventos meteoceanográficos são fundamentais para a operação eficiente do Plano Municipal Preventivo de Ressacas e Inundações Costeiras de Santos, instituído pelo Decreto Municipal Nº 7.804 de 06 de julho de 2017, apresentamos proposta para atualização da versão atual e continuidade de utilização dos serviços da plataforma AquaSafe que incluem: acesso aos dashboards com dados medidos por sensores e previsão de modelos, recebimento de boletins diários e semanais de previsão, monitoramento e validação da hidrodinâmica e da agitação marítima, atualização e manutenção contínua do sistema e emissão de boletins extraordinários de alertas de eventos extremos de ressacas marítimas em Santos.A plataforma AquaSafe Santos tem, portanto, por objetivo o aprimoramento e o fornecimento contínuo de um sistema de informações meteoceanográfico integrado para a cidade de Santos, em acordo com a necessidade do município de forma ampla e segura. Deve-se considerar como fator agravante os efeitos das mudanças climáticas, onde, conforme o Plano de Ação Climática de Santos (PACS), espera-se para o município um número cada vez maior de eventos extremos associados a chuvas e inundações costeiras. O custo total do projeto se refere a um período de 5 (cinco) anos.

column19: Os impactos econômicos, sociais e ambientais da mudança do clima são significativos no Brasil. Para responder a essa situação, o governo brasileiro tem desenvolvido uma agenda de adaptação à mudança do clima, cujo principal instrumento é o Plano Nacional de Adaptação (PNA). Os principais desafios para sua implementação nos níveis nacional, estadual e local são a falta de capacidade e de inovação metodológica. Além disso, a coordenação e o intercâmbio de experiências entre atores pertinentes no âmbito da adaptação à mudança do clima são insuficientes. Até o momento, existem poucos exemplos bem-sucedidos da integração do tema e de medidas concretas de adaptação no planejamento de políticas públicas e processos de tomada de decisão. Grande parte do esforço de adaptação deve vir de atores não governamentais e do setor privado. No entanto, em muitos casos, esses atores ainda desconhecem a necessidade de se adaptar à mudança do clima. O ProAdapta tem por objetivo reforçar a resiliência climática do Brasil por meio da implementação efetiva da Agenda Nacional de Adaptação à Mudança do Clima. O projeto será implementado em estreita cooperação com o Ministério do Meio Ambiente (MMA), fortalecendo sua função de coordenação com o auxílio de ferramentas de gestão, como o monitoramento de medidas de adaptação. Ao mesmo tempo, capacidades serão desenvolvidas nos setores, estados federais e municípios selecionados para implementação de políticas, de métodos e de instrumentos públicos para a integração de medidas replicáveis de adaptação à mudança do clima. O projeto também deve promover a adaptação do setor privado e da sociedade civil à mudança do clima por meio de medidas de conscientização e de sensibilização. Por fim, suas experiências de aprendizado serão disseminadas nacional e internacionalmente. A abordagem do projeto inclui a melhoraria das condições de enquadramento para adaptação à mudança do clima. O projeto deve fortalecer o Ministério do Meio Ambiente e outros atores governamentais na gestão dos riscos climáticos em políticas públicas, planos e programas. Por outro lado, o ProAdapta sensibiliza tomadores de decisão. Além disso, são desenvolvidas ferramentas para permitir a adaptação à mudança do clima e a integração desse tema nos processos de planejamento e de tomada de decisão. Experiências e abordagens de aprendizagem bem-sucedidas do projeto serão disseminadas e aplicadas em todo o Brasil como parte do processo de implementação do PNA (upscaling). Além disso, as experiências de aprendizado do ProAdapta também serão divulgadas nacional e internacionalmente.

column19: The City of Madison adopted a new Building Energy Savings Program (BESP) in 2023 to help large commercial building owners identify opportunities to increase energy efficiency, save money, and reduce the carbon footprint of their buildings, which currently account for 30% of community-wide greenhouse gas emissions. The new Building Energy Savings code aims to improve energy efficiency in large commercial buildings community-wide through energy benchmarking and tune-ups. Under the new code, non-residential commercial buildings 25,000 square feet and larger are required to benchmark energy use annually via EPA's Energy Star Portfolio Manager. Non-residential commercial buildings 50,000 square feet and larger will also be required to complete a building tune-up every four years. The program will provide the training, support, and information that building owners need to benchmark and tune up as well as take the next steps to turn building efficiency knowledge into action. Additional funding would be used to assist small business owners with this transition, perhaps providing incentives, and helping businesses from under-represented communities receive funding to help bridge the energy efficiency gap between their peers.

column17: Project not funded and seeking full funding
column19:
The Greensboro “Center for Environmental Education and Sustainability” is envisioned to be a will consist of five different components:
1.	A “swap shop” where construction and demolition (C&D) waste materials can be offered for re-use to the public free-of-charge. A Sustainable Materials Management (SMM) approach will be used in order to identify C&D materials that can be re-used or repurposed, including:
a)	Lumber - Sorted (treated and untreated) and de-nailed. Reusable lumber would be staged in the swap shop for public use. Unusable untreated lumber would be processed into mulch or compost. Unusable treated lumber would be sent to the city's C&D waste landfill.
b)	Metal - Sorted and containerized for resale to a local metal recycling company.
c)	Drywall - Would be processed to remove the exterior paper, nails, and other metal, leaving only gypsum. The gypsum would be incorporated into the city's compost and mulch operations, used in the onsite community garden, sold in bulk to residents for home gardening, or sold to landscaping or drywall companies.
d)	Concrete/brick/block - Whole usable units would be made available to the public for re-use. Broken units would be crushed and made available to the public for re-use as paving or landscaping material.
e)	Asphalt shingles - Tar paper and shingles would be de-nailed and staged for transport to an asphalt recycling facility or used as an alternate fuel source (e.g., cement kilns).
f)	Glass - Would be transported to the city's glass recycling center.
2.	A satellite Household Hazardous Waste (HHW) drop-off location; 
3.	A firewood bank, where pre-split firewood will be made available free-of-charge to the public, including individuals and families lacking permanent shelter.
4.	A working community garden with over 50 raised beds (12 - 15 will be ADA accessible). Ten of the raised beds will be reserved at-risk youth counselling and rehabilitation purposes.
5.	An educational facility which will be available for classes on community gardening and composting, solid waste and recycling, landfill construction, maintenance, and operation, clean renewable energy sources, bee-keeping, native plant landscaping, canning and food storage, sustainable building design and construction, and other related topics. In addition to classes organized and led by city staff, the facility would also host classes presented by other organizations such as K-12 schools, colleges and universities, civic groups, etc.
6.	Administrative offices and meeting space for the Office of Sustainability and Resilience.

column19: The “Flooding and Drainage Improvement Framework”: https://www.hamilton.ca/city-council/plans-strategies/master-plans-studies/flooding-and-drainage-master-servicing-study Was initiated in the summer of 2021 and has involved a holistic review of the City's combined sewer system, with the goal of developing a framework that outlines a long-term management strategy to address existing flooding and drainage issues. The Framework has been structured to provide a high-level roadmap and actionable next steps for the City to better plan for a program of long-term capital improvements and to coordinate these improvements and upgrades within the combined sewer system. The main purpose of the Framework has been to review the combined sewer system, on a sewershed basis, in order to establish a better understanding of the local system's configuration, performance, and potential contributors to flooding, leading to an identification of priorities including potential short and long-term infrastructure solutions. This framework has laid the groundwork for several Municipal Class Environmental Assessments (EAs), which will ultimately identify which infrastructure solutions should be designed and built to mitigate combined sewer overflow discharges, significantly reduce basement flooding events, and improve local surface water quality over a long-term implementation plan. Options such as sewer separation and green infrastructure will be evaluated within the EA studies throughout the combined sewershed in Hamilton, implemented over a 30+ year period.

column19: Better Homes Hamilton (BHH): https://engage.hamilton.ca/betterhomeshamilton The City of Hamilton is on a mission to acheive net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 2050. To do this City Council approved the design and development of a Home Energy Retrofit Program Opportunity, previously known as HERO, has now been rebranded as the Better Homes Hamilton program. The Better Homes Hamilton (BHH) program is meant to provide a low barrier access to property owners with upfront capital in order to retrofit their buildings to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, improve energy efficiency, and to live more comfortably.The pilot program first targeting up to 50 homes with an initial investment from the City of Hamilton of $1.0M was approved by City Council in May 2023 and anticipated to launch before the end of 2023. However has per Hamilton's Community Energy and Emissions Plan, Low-Carbon Transformation #2: Transforming our Buildings, almost every building in Hamilton will need to be retrofitted. Therefore moving forward the building retrofit program will need to be scaled across the City to reach more homeowners and different building sectors including Multi-Unit Residential, Commercial and Industrial.

The overall goal of BetterHomes London is to encourage more home energy retrofits to take place making use of all available incentive programs as well as offer lower-interest LIC-based loans to around 150 households. Civic Administration anticipate that many, if not most homeowners, may wish to use their own sources of financing (e.g., line of credit, Tax-Free Savings Account) for simplicity. 

The FCM's Community Efficiency Financing Loan and Grant Agreement will provide the City of London with a $1,772,929 grant to be used for program start-up and operating costs, and a $3,545,859 loan contribution toward the pool of loan capital to be used by Londoners to access low-interest loans paid back though property tax payments through the Local Improvement Charge process. The City of London is providing a $1,500,000 recoverable contribution toward the pool of loan capital to be accessed by Londoners and repaid to the City of London as included in the adopted 2024-2027 Multi-Year Budget. Overall, this represents a 3.5:1 (three and a half to one) leveraging of the City of London's financial contribution. 

Current program design assumptions presume that it will take four years to reach the program goal of issuing 150 home energy retrofit loans, but the actual pace of loan issuance will depend on demand. If program loan uptake is faster than anticipated, the FCM Community Efficiency Financing grants for program operation remain in place for the full four years of program operation. Tools and services available through the BetterHomes London program, such as the concierge service, would remain in place to encourage more home energy retrofits through conventional financing.

Based on program funding and potential financing arrangements, program deliverables over four years could include the following:

•	About 150 households using property-assessed low-interest loans of around $33,000 on average through the LIC mechanism;
•	About 75 low-to-middle income households receiving an additional incentive of $5,000 on average to assist with retrofits; and
•	About 25 households receiving an additional incentive of $5,000 on average to assist with Net-Zero Ready retrofits.

column19: The proposed project, a permanently installed, islandable microgrid, will provide back-up power to support the critical functions of the Civic Center including the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) facilities during extended power outages caused by catastrophic events (earthquake, wildfire, storms, etc.) while reducing greenhouse gases and making the Civic Center Zero Net Energy. Greater grid resiliency allows the City of Chula Vista to manage risk and increase public safety in their community. The Civic Center Energy Hub will prove that external Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) can be coordinated and controlled centrally to achieve multiple objectives. Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) for the Energy Hub include energy efficiency, advanced lighting and HVAC controls to enable additional demand response capabilities, energy storage, coordination with existing PV and EV Charging, and installation and configuration of a microgrid controller to monitor, control and optimize the operation of all DERs. In the event of a regional power outage, it is crucial that the Civic Center retain the ability to function and perform critical services to the Community. The ability to operate ensures public safety services, prevents costly accidents and health hazards, and avoids a break in service associated with the outage. In the event of a disaster caused outage, a microgrid at the Civic Center would allow it to disconnect from the utility grid, effectively turning itself into a self-sustaining energy island, allowing functions at the Civic Center to continue, such as sending signals to traffic lights, dispatching emergency personnel, operating the emergency operations center, provide shelter and cool zones, and delivering critical services to the community. Because the Civic Center serves a disadvantaged community, it is especially critical to maintain normal City functions during grid outages. Staff and partners have applied for multiple grants for this project over the last several years and we are hopeful we can eventually secure grant funding for this project. We have mainly been applying for funds from various state agencies, to date. Staff have also recently considered the potential for financing for this project. While the microgrid would be located at the Civic Center campus, the entire community would gain the benefits of climate resiliency as critical services (EMS transport services, public safety dispatch, EOC headquarters, cooling centers, emergency food distribution, Information Technology Services, municipal electric fleet charging, the free Chula Vista Community EV Shuttle service, free Bayfront EV Shuttle, etc.) would continue to function to serve the city.

This project involves the phased replacement of internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles with electric vehicles (EVs), beginning in the 2026/2027 budget cycle. An Electric Vehicle Roadmap, approved in 2025, outlines the purchase of 328 EVs over a 16-year period. The first 195 EVs will replace existing ICE vehicles, resulting in an estimated reduction of 13,893 tonnes of CO₂e emissions.

While electric vehicles have a higher upfront purchase cost and require charging infrastructure and potential electrical system upgrades, they offer significant long-term savings through reduced fuel and maintenance expenses. According to the Roadmap, the total cost of ownership (TCO) for an EV is projected to be $101,000 higher than a comparable ICE vehicle over its lifecycle.

Given the environmental benefits and alignment with sustainable investment criteria, this initiative is a potential candidate for Green Loan financing. To offset the incremental costs associated with the loan and the higher TCO, the project will also seek federal grant funding.

column15: Phase 2: Decarbonization Project for the Como Park Zoo & Conservatory Campus
column17: Project partially funded and seeking additional funding
column18: Grants|Public finance- national government|Other: Energy Savings Performance Contract
column19: The City of Saint Paul - Como Park Zoo & Conservatory is the most visited cultural attraction in Minnesota with 1.7 million annual visitors and is free to the public. With 25% of the visitors coming from Greater Minnesota, the Como Zoo is an economic engine that provides $162.7 million dollars in economic impact to the State of Minnesota and generates 2,093 jobs. On an annual basis, over 400,000 students participate in programs and field trips.The Como Park Zoo & Conservatory campus has the highest energy consumption within the City of Saint Paul's municipal building portfolio, spending over $1 million annually on energy costs. The City originally set a goal to reduce energy costs at Como Park & Zoo 20% from 2013 levels by 2020, and worked closely with Xcel Energy to complete recommissioning studies and develop a Joint Energy Efficiency Plan that identified a wide range of energy efficiency measures that could achieve that energy reduction goal within a 5-year timeframe. Due to funding and workforce limitations over the past few years, most of those energy conservation measures still need to be implemented. The adoption of the City of Saint Paul's Climate Action & Resilience Plan in 2019 established the goal for municipal operations to be carbon neutral by 2030, so more ambitious decarbonization efforts at the Como Park & Zoo campus are now necessary. A geothermal feasibility study was completed for the Como Park & Zoo campus in 2022, and the City was able to secure $2.2 million in federal funds to install a Hydro Geothermal Heat Pump (HGHP) at the Primates/Gorilla Building in 2024 The City is currently exploring opportunities for a larger-scale decarbonization project that would transition the zoo campus off of the inefficient natural gas-powered steam system. This project would use an Energy Savings Performance Contract (ESPC) approach to implement energy efficiency measures at 10-15 zoo buildings and could include Hydro Geothermal Heat Pump installations at an additional 1 or 2 buildings. The decarbonization project at the Como Park & Zoo campus could cost between $15 million to $48 million, depending on the project scope, but would result in significant energy savings and carbon emissions reductions at the campus.

The cities of Saint Paul and Minneapolis are partnering to seek funding that would enable us to expand our successful electric carshare program and substantially reduce emissions from transportation in the Twin Cities region. In 2022 Saint Paul and Minneapolis launched
the EV Spot Network. This network provides publicly owned electric vehicle carshare + chargers:
§ Evie Carshare: Today, residents can check out 170 shared electric vehicles and return them to any legal on-street parking space across 35 square miles. This is generally called 'one-way' carshare because people can take the car one way and leave it at their destination. Users do not need to return the car to where they started.
§ EV Spot Charging: Today, residents can use 70 EV Spots to charge electric vehicles. The cities contract with regional utility Xcel Energy so that these chargers provide 100% zero-GHG, renewable energy.
Our system works. In 2023, residents of Minneapolis-Saint Paul used Evie Carshare to make 123,000 zero-emission trips—to the doctor, to buy groceries, to see their families. Evie Carshare is equitably serving those who need it most: in 2023, 43% of utilization came from Black, Indigenous, People of Color (BIPOC)/non-white users, and 43% by very low-income users. Together, in 2023 Evie Carshare and its users reduced 4,424 metric tons (mT) of CO2e. As a result of this rapid growth, the current Evie Carshare system is near its capacity. Demand often exceeds the available number of cars. 
Expansion of the areas served, the number of EV cars in the fleet and the number of available charging hubs is proposed to meet the demand.

column19: Retention Treatment Basin (RTB) across the Lou Romano Water Reclamation Plant Stantec Consulting Ltd. completed the Windsor Riverfront West CSO Control Schedule C Environmental Assessment on July 17, 2019. It investigated and identified means for controlling combined sewer overflows (CSOs) along the Windsor waterfront between Caron Avenue and the LRWRP as well as wet weather control at the Lou Romano Water Reclamation Plant (LRWRP). A retention treatment basin at Lou Romano Water Reclamation Plant, and associated works, are the preferred alternative. An auxiliary but important aspect of the work is that this CSO control alternative also will result in reduced water levels at the inlet chamber to the LRWRP during severe storm events. It will also alleviate the high-water conditions and reduce risk for basement flooding in the areas served by the Western Main Trunk Sewer, which serves South Windsor. This project will have a significant impact yielding ROI results of 53.37:1, based one-third of the benefiting area impacted by a rain event, and 160.09:1, based on 100% of the benefitting area impacted by a rain event. The ROI calculation meets the requirements of the grant application. The ROI for the RTB is significant due to the number of homes in the drainage area (approximately 40,000 with basement) and the improvements to level of service under the 1:5 year, 1:100 year and climate change storm scenarios.

O Projeto Ajuémangue tem como objetivo a produção de mudas de espécies nativas de mangue no município de Aracaju, com foco na recuperação de áreas degradadas dos ecossistemas estuarinos e na promoção da educação ambiental. Diante dos crescentes impactos das mudanças climáticas, como a elevação do nível do mar, a intensificação de eventos extremos e a perda de biodiversidade, a restauração dos manguezais se torna uma ação estratégica para a adaptação e resiliência climática.

Esses ecossistemas atuam como importantes sumidouros de carbono, protegem as zonas costeiras contra erosões e tempestades, além de manterem serviços ecossistêmicos essenciais à vida humana. Considerando que o manguezal é também um dos principais símbolos da identidade ecológica e cultural da cidade, a iniciativa busca envolver ativamente a população local, especialmente comunidades ribeirinhas, escolas e grupos socioambientais, no processo de coleta de sementes, cultivo, cuidado e plantio das mudas. 

A proposta reforça o sentimento de pertencimento e responsabilidade coletiva pela preservação do mangue, fomentando práticas sustentáveis, disseminando conhecimento e fortalecendo a conexão entre o povo aracajuano e o seu patrimônio natural diante dos desafios climáticos do presente e do futuro.

column17: Other: Project fully funded
column19: The proposed stormwater improvements will address chronic flooding within this historic neighborhood of Fort Lauderdale. When this neighborhood was originally developed, graded grass swale areas along the roadways were used as the primary method for handling stormwater runoff from the public right of way areas. Over time, these graded grass swale areas within the public right of way have accumulated sediments from stormwater runoff, become overgrown with vegetation, and been eliminated by the installation of extensive landscaping, paved parking lanes, expanded driveway approaches, and other hardscape elements throughout the Victoria Park neighborhood. The reduction and elimination of graded grass swale areas throughout the neighborhood has reduced the storage capacity and infiltration capacity for stormwater runoff generated within and/or draining to the public right of way and has led to ponding issues within roadway areas during and after rainfall events. The project scope for the Victoria Park Stormwater Flood Improvements project will be to replace the aging, undersized and fragmented stormwater infrastructure with a comprehensive system that will help with flooding in the neighborhood and water quality treatment prior to being discharged into the Intracoastal Waterways. The improvements will include 24,380 linear feet (LF) of stormwater pipe, 19,000 (LF) of exfiltration trenches, 10,000 square yards (SY) of new swales, and 120 (LF) of seawall replacements. Lastly, the system will also include a stormwater pump station that will be capable of draining the low-lying eastern areas of Victoria Park neighborhood during elevated high tide events and/or projected sea level rise scenarios. The stormwater improvements proposed to alleviate the flooding have been designed and permitted through all appropriate agencies and it currently being packaged to go out to bid for construction. This is a shovel-ready project will take approximately 2-years to construct once a contractor is procured.

The City of Tempe is seeking funding to install solar and battery storage systems (microgrids) at municipal and community-serving facilities. This effort builds on a soon to be completed Microgrid Master Plan, which assessed the energy needs, electrical capacity, and system requirements for each site.

The plan identifies priority buildings across the city, including 10 fire and police facilities, 7 community centers, that are well-suited for microgrid installation. These facilities are critical to Tempe's resilience strategy, helping to maintain power during grid outages and provide community support during extreme heat and emergency events.

With system sizing, energy modeling, and cost estimates already almost completed, the city is now pursuing funding to implement the installations. In addition to city-owned sites, Tempe's Sustainability and Resilience Division is working with faith-based organizations (who were also part of this feasibility study) to help them identify and secure funding for microgrid projects at their own sites, particularly those located in heat-priority neighborhoods and trusted by local residents.

The City of Tempe is seeking funding to transition its Orbit Neighborhood Circulator fleet to zero-emission, battery-electric buses (BEBs). 

In April 2025, the city in partnership with National Renewable Energy Laboratory, finished its Orbit Neighborhood Circulator Zero-Emission Fleet Transition Plan. The plan addresses current and future resource availability and costs associated with the transition and implementation of the Orbit fleet, as this service is not included in regional transition plans. The plan also explores the partnerships and training required to make the transition possible. 

Tempe aims to replace its existing diesel and CNG buses with 44 electric vehicles and install the charging infrastructure needed to support daily operations. The transition timeline is aligned with the natural replacement cycle of the current fleet and could be completed between 2026 and 2034, depending on funding and coordination with local utilities.

To support implementation, Tempe has already:

- Identified vehicle and charging needs
- Assessed electrical capacity at key transit facilities
- Developed a phased procurement and infrastructure installation plan


Through a separate yet related effort, the City partnered with Arizona Public Services (APS) to identity infrastructure and utility needs to fulfill ZEB needs at the City's East Valley Bus Operations and Maintenance Facility and Tempe Transportation Center sites. 

The City is now actively pursuing funding to purchase electric buses, upgrade facilities, and build out charging infrastructure. Funding is not yet secured to complete these initiatives. Staff will continue to pursue funding opportunities.

A food action plan for sustainability is a strategic document that outlines steps to create a food system to address challenges like food insecurity, climate change, and resource depletion within the food system.

Goals related to the Food Action Plan will include:

- stakeholder engagement
- promoting sustainable agriculture
- reducing food waste
- improving access to healthy food
- supporting local food businesses
- advocating for supportive policies

Benefits of a food action plan for sustainability include:

- environmental benefits (reduced greenhouse gas emissions, improved soil health, increased biodiversity, and water conservation)
- social benefits (increased food security, improved nutrition)
- economic benefits (new business opportunities, reduced costs associated with food waste)

DASH is the first transit agency inNorthern Virginia to deploy electric buses. The City and DASH have completed the first phase of a Zero Emission BusImplementation Study which will provide a detailed, strategic roadmap to transition the entire fleet by approximately FY 2037.The second phase of this study is expected to be completed by late 2022.For FY 2023, DASH has 15 buses that will have reached the end of their useful life and are eligible for replacement; however,due to funding constraints, DASH is only requesting 8 clean diesel replacement buses. column19: Over 10 years ago, the City of Grand Rapids began exploring installing solar panels on the Butterworth Landfill, which is a 190-acre Superfund site where cleanup was completed in 2000. Due to the protective cap that was installed and cannot be disturbed, ground mounted solar panels, an open field or a paved parking lot are the only viable beneficial reuses of the property. In 2013, the EPA completed a solar reuse assessment and found that the Butterworth Landfill is well-suited for solar power generation due to the relatively flat, open and unobstructed surface of the site as well as plenty of sun exposure and close proximity to necessary electricity infrastructure. In that assessment, the EPA determined that 63 acres were viable for solar installation. The City entered into a contract with a solar developer in 2015 for an approximately 2.5 megawatt DC array in the southwest corner of the landfill that was intended to go over or under the river and supply the City's Water Resource Recovery Facility (WRRF). The developer ultimately went bankrupt and the project fell through. In the last year, the City has revitalized its efforts to develop the site and has developed a multi-project approach. The City first plans to develop the optimal amount of solar-powered electricity at the site behind-the-meter to the City-owned and operated Primary Circuit (PC). The City will maximize direct benefits to the Grand Rapids community through emissions reductions, air pollution reduction, affordability, electrification, jobs, etc. and demonstrate innovative approaches to the deployment of solar in conjunction with interpretive/educational uses. The City intends to deploy up to a 2MW solar array to support the Primary Circuit. The City has already initiated and completed the RFI/RFQ phase of this component and has 10 qualified solar developers participating in workshopping of next steps toward a formal RFP in late Spring/early Summer. In addition, the City's Engineering Department is currently at 30% design for the PC extension required to connect the array. Michigan currently has no enabling legislation for privately developed community solar. However, the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) approved the Solar Gardens Sunrise program within Consumers Energy's (CE) Voluntary Green Pricing program; The Community Solar component of this project is designed to provide 3,520MWh of solar electricity annually to low income and disadvantaged communities within the city of Grand Rapids via a 5MW array with a 30-year life expectancy. This component of the project is estimated to cost $14.7 million, with $12.5 million accounting for capital costs associated with constructing 5MW of solar. The remaining amount of requested funding for this component supports hiring a full time solar specialist (this person will manage all three measures of the grant), a subaward with a qualified non-profit that will manage household participation in the program, a subaward with community partners to create and facilitate a Solar Justice Team, funding for the development of a Grand Rapids-based solar career development program, and enrollment costs for 30 people to participate in the training program. The third component of the project is installation of an 8MW solar array that would serve the City's district energy/steam district. The persistent challenge across the globe in electrifying steam/district energy systems has been twofold. First, the capital costs of reinvesting in and retrofitting existing plants can be challenging. The second - and perhaps greater - challenge is the fuel cost differential between traditional natural gas and electricity, which can be 6x-10x. Fortunately, Vicinity has made a commitment to investments on the former, while this public-private PV partnership can help to address the latter. Vicinity Energy (Vicinity) owns and operates the district energy system in Grand Rapids and serves approximately 120 buildings in the downtown core. It operates under a franchise tariff with the City of Grand Rapids as its regulating authority. The system provides gas-fueled steam heating for over 10 million square feet of space, including residential buildings, hospitals, colleges/ universities, municipal and commercial office buildings, the arena, convention center, hotels, churches, non-profits, restaurants, and retail facilities.

At present, utility data is stored across multiple departments and platforms, while facility GHG emissions are calculated manually in spreadsheets—an approach that is time-intensive, increases the risk of errors, and slows both real-time and long-term decision-making.

Such a system could reduce annual utility costs by 10% or more by enabling staff to act quickly on real-time data, prevent billing errors, and verify energy savings from efficiency projects (e.g., LED lighting upgrades, building retrofits). column19: Imagine a resident-designed home energy audit that centers people, comfort, safety, and health. Imagine that assessment being piloted in a single low-income neighborhood such that identified needs can be aggregated and bulk discounts and improvements negotiated to help frontline populations immediately improve health, safety, comfort, and reduce energy bills. That's what we aim to do through a partnership with residents in the Bryant neighborhood, the Community Action Network, Bryant Community Center, the City of Ann Arbor, Elevate, home energy auditors, and contractors conducting home repair, weatherization, electrification, and solar installations. Located in the south of Ann Arbor, the Bryant neighborhood is defined as the roughly 260 households that are served by the Bryant Community Center - a community center run by the Community Action Network with support from the City of Ann Arbor. All the houses in the neighborhood were built by the same developer and only two archetypes exist - making extrapolation and comparison of opportunities possible across the neighborhood. The Bryant neighborhood is one of the City's largest low-income neighborhoods. Of the 260 households, about 75% are considered low-income, 50% are owner occupied, and the majority of residents are People of Color. In 2020, the City approached the McKnight Foundation and secured a planning grant to work with residents in the Bryant neighborhood, along with Community Action Network, to co-design a whole home health, safety, comfort, and decarbonization assessment specifically to improve indoor air quality, resident comfort, and to advance the City's goals of achieving a just transition to community-wide carbon neutrality by 2030 (known as A2ZERO). This work began in April 2021 and has already uncovered many opportunities to improve indoor air quality and improve resident safety and health, while also highlighting many of the unique and charming elements of the Bryant neighborhood that are valued by residents. With information highlighted through these initial assessments, Ann Arbor and the project team has obtained around $5 million spread throughout a few grants and is seeking more funds to complete implementation a district geothermal installation that has been designed in collaboration with residents and geothermal experts. The funding to-date is enough to work on around 120 of the 262 homes. The Department of Energy has also awarded Ann Arbor $10 million to install the district geothermal system, but with the Federal budget situation, those funds have yet to be allocated. Michigan's relatively low cost of natural gas and high cost of electricity makes these improvements difficult to complete without external funding, despite the clear benefits to the community and beyond. The data generated by the project around energy efficiency, air quality, public health, work force development, comfort, safety, and more benefits, along with the unique community engagement strategy, can be collected to replicate in other neighborhoods, cities, and regions.

column15: Reduce, Reuse, Return: Establishing a City-Scale Returnable Foodware Program in Ann Arbor
column17: Project not funded and seeking full funding
column19: The global crisis of single-use plastics has reached a critical point, with over 8 million tons of plastic entering our oceans each year (United Nations, 2017). Of particular concern is plastic food contact packaging, which not only poses risks to human health through the leaching of harmful chemicals like bisphenols and phthalates, but also contributes to the widespread contamination of our soil and waterways with microplastics (Gore et al., 2024). These tiny plastic particles now permeate ecosystems and even infiltrate the food and water we consume, raising alarm about long-term impacts on public health and the environment (World Health Organization, 2019). This project will demonstrate one meaningful pathway to address these concerns by creating a City-wide returnable foodware container program to be used in Ann Arbor's restaurants, venues, institutions, and public schools - thereby replacing single-use plastics. Designed in collaboration between the Ann Arbor Office of Sustainability and Innovations, the Ecology Center, Perpetual, and local restaurants, grocers, food vendors, and community institutions, this program will demonstrate how to drastically reduce plastic waste while stimulating a more circular economy and healthier natural systems. This will be done by providing at least 150 area restaurants and institutions, including K-12 schools and college campus locations, with reusable food and beverage containers to replace single use plastics, developing and operating a centralized station that washes, dries, and transports these containers, and building the social infrastructure, including business training, community engagement, and public education, to ensure that this initiative achieves the adoption necessary to become the preeminent form of consuming foods and beverages in Ann Arbor. By eliminating six million single-use food and beverage containers during the project timeline - and developing the infrastructure to expand this initiative for years to come - this project will directly address the environmental and human health impacts of plastic pollution within the project area, including concerns associated with microplastics within the Huron River. The Huron River, located within the project area, is the area's primary source of drinking water, and is frequently used by members of the community for recreation, including swimming and kayaking, A 2016 study conducted by the US Geological Survey found that the Huron River had the highest rate of microplastic pollution of any of the 29 Great Lakes tributaries that were tested. With extreme rain events increasing by 37% over the last 30 years in Ann Arbor, marine plastic and microplastic pollution are only expected to increase as heavy rains carry single-use plastics into the area's waterways with increased frequency and severity. Further, this project addresses human health impacts associated with plastic and microplastic pollution, namely the adverse respiratory impacts of fine particle pollution. Of the 24 EPA IRA Disadvantaged Community ID tracts that comprise the project area, all but two are in the top quartile for adult asthma rates, with 15 ranking in the 92nd percentile or higher, making both the environment and people who comprise the community outlined in the project area disparately vulnerable to plastic pollution. Learn more about the program here: https://zerowaste.org/ann-arbor/returnables

column19: The City of Ann Arbor is working to expand composting access for multi-family residents by establishing a network of food scrap drop-off sites and promoting curbside collection for smaller multi-family properties already located on existing service routes. The creation of the new food scrap drop-off sites will extend a more convenient way for the roughly 50% of City residents living in multi-family housing to recycle their food scraps. While Ann Arbor has long offered curbside food scrap collection for single-family homes, limited resources have largely prevented the expansion of this service to multifamily housing, aside from a few pilot properties. A comprehensive analysis of the size, type, and location of multi-family housing along with expected generation and participation rates yielded the establishment of a drop-off system to be the most efficient and cost-effective way to extend food scrap collection to multi-family households, especially to those living larger (greater than ten units) properties. Specifically, the establishment of twenty drop-off sites will put 98% of multi-family parcels within one mile of a drop-off location. Smaller properties of less than ten units will be encouraged to obtain a cart from the City for curbside collection. The requested funding will support the purchase of tech-enabled cart enclosures, curbside compost carts in three sizes, and a specialized organic waste truck. The tech-enabled enclosures are key to creating unstaffed drop-off sites, as they will keep the cart locked until accessed by a registered user. Each drop-off site will either house a 64-gallon or 35-gallon cart inside an enclosure, while 96-gallon carts will be provided to smaller multi-family properties eligible for curbside service. The specialized organic waste truck will be equipped to service and wash up to three carts at a time, which is essential for maintaining sanitary, low-maintenance drop-off sites without needing a separate cleaning service. This project addresses a primary source of greenhouse gas emissions by reducing the amount of food waste sent to our local landfill. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports that food waste accounts for 58 percent of methane emissions from municipal solid waste landfills. By redirecting food waste to composting, the city addresses this significant source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. The EPA's Wasted Food Scale indicates that composting is the most environmentally beneficial option for food that cannot be used for human or animal consumption, thereby making this project a key strategy in reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

column15: Food Waste Reduction & Composting Educational Campaign
column17: Project not funded and seeking full funding
column19: The City of Ann Arbor seeks to develop and provide a robust educational campaign to all residents about the importance of food waste reduction and composting. The over-arching goal of this project is to prevent household food waste from being landfilled. The primary objectives that will allow us to reach this goal include 1) developing a city-wide food waste reduction educational campaign, and 2) providing up to 25% of the city's households with food waste starter kits. A city-wide educational campaign will focus on both food waste reduction as well as the importance of composting. The messaging is intended to pull from resources provided by the NRDC “Save the Food Campaign” regarding proper food storage, meal planning, and how to use food that is about to spoil. We want our residents to think first about reducing how much waste they generate, and then take the most responsible action with any waste that remains. In the case of food scraps, we encourage composting as the sustainable disposal action. To support this effort, the City will hire a campaign content creator to develop messaging, outreach materials, and visuals tailored to our local audience. Key deliverables include the development of a short booklet containing information such as practical tips for proper food storage, food preservation, and meal planning that will be direct mailed to every residential address in the city. This campaign will be complemented by the distribution of 14,400 food waste starter kits—reaching approximately 25% of the city's households. Each kit will include a countertop food scrap caddy, a magnet with food storage tips, fridge and freezer labels, and a postcard explaining how to register for and use the new food scrap drop-off program. At events where starter kits will be distributed, the City will also provide finished compost from its facility for residents to take home. Since these kits will be aimed at multi-family residents who likely do not have a yard, small paper pouches will be available for them to collect a reasonable amount for use in potted plants and small flower beds. The project is designed to help residents understand and participate in the full cycle of food waste management from prevention to composting, to soil improvement.

In order to increase existing local capacity, decrease contamination, and improve efficiency of collection for the recovery of clean cardboard from the City's commercial recycling customers, the City will purchase cardboard compactors, work with businesses to install them at key collection points and purchase an associated collection truck to serve the compactors and increased demand for recycling collection. This project will reduce waste to landfill and improve collection efficiencies.
The City of Ann Arbor has provided recycling collection to commercial businesses for over 20 years, yet we know we are missing some materials as evidenced in the State of Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy's (EGLE) 2024 Waste Composition study, that found 16.5% of commercial trash is cardboard. Anecdotally, City crews observe unflattened boxes in recycling. Additionally, the City contracted with a local non-profit, The Ecology Center (EC), to provide direct education to our commercial customers. In the first year, EC worked with 9 businesses in 4 shopping centers, while in year 2 they worked with 40 businesses in 13 shopping centers. The businesses were a mix of retail, service, and restaurants, each with 1 to over 50 employees. Prior to engaging each business, EC completed a visual assessment of trash, recycle, and any compost containers. They noted percent full, composition, relative percentage of different materials, specific contaminants, and whether boxes were flattened. Then they engaged with the employees directly including on-site interviews and training followed by 1 or 2 more visual assessments. 

Results show that in year 1 of the contract, 2 of the 4 shopping centers (50%) had cardboard in their trash, and 2 (50%) had unflattened boxes in their recycling. In year 2 of the contract, 6 of the 13 shopping centers (46%) had cardboard in their trash, 3 (23%) did not have enough capacity for their cardboard, and 9 (69%) had unflattened boxes in their dumpsters. It was noted that cardboard in 96-gallon carts was regularly flat. One shopping center had a cardboard baler and there was no contamination noted in their recycling. The diversity of businesses engaged by the Ecology Center is representative of the businesses throughout the city, making their data a good reference for our commercial customers overall. To address issues with capacity, not flattening boxes, and boxes in the trash, the City proposes to install cardboard compactors at 15 strategic locations identified with high need. A truck will be purchased to service the compactors and to add collection capacity to the City's fleet to help meet an increasing demand for service as the city grows and adds more development. This ties to the national recycling strategy by increasing collection and improving materials management infrastructure. A consultant would be hired to manage and report on the grant and develop and implement the cardboard compactor program.

column15: Sub-award infrastructure grants to local non-profits and service organization involved in materials reuse
column17: Project not funded and seeking full funding
column19:
This project aims to support greater recovery of usable goods during annual student move out events. Specifically, it will provide sub-award infrastructure grants to local non-profits and service organizations involved in materials reuse in order to increase collection. This project will reduce waste to landfill and keep goods in circulation. 

The City of Ann Arbor has a deep and extensive reuse network already in place that serves the county as well as the city. However, as Ann Arbor is a university town, there remains a significant opportunity to recover materials left behind by students and provide them to people in need. Ann Arbor's population is approximately 125,000; about 30% or 37,000 are off-campus students. These students are very transient and produce an estimated additional 1,400 tons of municipal solid waste annually during May and August move-outs. The University of Michigan offers collection for reuse to on-campus residents and collected about 11 tons of materials in Spring 2024. An area non-profit collected 14 tons from off-campus housing for reuse, specifically to furnish homes for those coming out of homelessness. Additionally, the City runs a temporary drop off site for reuse, recycling, and trash that in 2024 diverted 24 tons of material for reuse and recycling. However, there is still a lot of untapped potential, and the City strives to do more with it. 

To determine how to further increase collection and improve material management pathways for materials left behind by students, the City researched 27 universities and towns and spoke with 6 of them about their relevant programs. From this we learned: 1) many and diverse partners are needed, 2) many and diverse material streams can be addressed, and 3) outreach needs to be comprehensive, institutionalized, frequent, and through many channels. With this research, we formed Move Out Ann Arbor (MOAA), a collaborative initiative to improve the recovery and reuse of unwanted materials to the benefit of communities facing adverse disproportionate health, environmental, climate-related, and economic impacts. We met 8 times in 2024 and are building upon the many existing services by creating synergies and connections. Our partners include various departments at the university, property managers, non-profit reuse/service organizations, and waste haulers. 

In addition to the MOAA work of meeting, creating connections, and piloting some management pathways, the City has done extensive engagement to understand the landscape and timing. We have spoken with property managers/landlords, students, the Panhellenic Group, communities of faith, the Inter-Cooperative Council, and area non-profit reuse/service organizations. We have learned that there are already many non-profits in this space with well-aligned goals and services. For example, House N2 Home gathers materials left behind by students to help furnish approximately 400 homes in 2024 for people transitioning from homelessness. Their clients are referred to them from 40 other service organizations. House N2 Home then works with all their clients to ensure their new home reflects their tastes, preferences, and style as much as possible. When the client comes to their new home, House N2 Home has completely furnished it and provided a home cooked meal, dessert, flowers, and a card. These non-profits need additional support to expand and grow their efforts at recovering materials for reuse. For example, House N2 Home has expressed they could do more if they had an additional box truck for pickups and deliveries. We have also learned from property managers/landlords that timing is very important, with a typical 2-week window of opportunity between students leaving and new students moving in. 

To further support the National Recycling Strategy of enhancing policies and programs to support circularity, we propose to have sub-award grants for infrastructure for area non-profits/service organizations to deliver materials left behind by students to adversely impacted communities. Based on our engagement thus far, these non-profits are interested in items like box trucks to transport materials, supplies/containers to collect and transport materials, and leased or purchased containers for material storage or other warehousing. This ties to the National Recycling Strategy by increasing collection and improving materials management infrastructure. A consultant would be hired to manage and report on the grant and would also complete program development and management of the reuse sub-award grants.

To determine how to further increase collection and improve material management pathways for materials left behind by students, the City researched 27 universities and towns and spoke with 6 of them about their relevant programs. From this we learned: 1) many and diverse partners are needed, 2) many and diverse material streams can be addressed, and 3) outreach needs to be comprehensive, institutionalized, frequent, and through many channels. With this research, we formed Move Out Ann Arbor (MOAA), a collaborative initiative to improve the recovery and reuse of unwanted materials to the benefit of communities facing adverse disproportionate health, environmental, climate-related, and economic impacts. We met 8 times in 2024 and are building upon the many existing services by creating synergies and connections. Our partners include various departments at the university, property managers, non-profit reuse/service organizations, and waste haulers. 
 
In addition to the MOAA work of meeting, creating connections, and piloting some management pathways, the City has done extensive engagement to understand the landscape and timing. We have spoken with property managers/landlords, students, the Panhellenic Group, communities of faith, the Inter-Cooperative Council, and area non-profit reuse/service organizations. We have learned that there are already many non-profits in this space with well-aligned goals and services. These non-profits need additional support to expand and grow their efforts at recovering materials for reuse. We have also learned from property managers/landlords that timing is very important, with a typical 2-week window of opportunity between students leaving and new students moving in. 
 
To further support the National Recycling Strategy of enhancing policies and programs to support circularity, we propose to create a reuse software tool that will connect those with materials to those who need them. The vision for this software is to be like Uber or Instacart where there is near on-demand collection service to help meet the high volume of materials generated from turning over apartments within a 2-week timeframe by allowing students to post unwanted items and have our non-profit network and volunteers claim the items for pick-up. The tool would provide a more “real-time” service than posting an item on a Buy-Nothing Group, Facebook Marketplace or the like. Those existing tools do not ensure items will be collected in a defined time frame, where the proposed new tool would give that assurance to the person posting. There is an added benefit to organizations doing collection, as the tool would allow them a better means of routing collection stops to maximize the time, they have available to do this work. In addition to increasing collection capacity for reuse and supporting circular economy programs, the software will also standardize metrics and increase data collection of diverted goods/materials by integrating data collection into the tool. To track the impact of reuse, the software tool would include average weights for common household goods and suggested methodology for weighing items such as a bag of linens or clothes. These weights could then be aggregated across all recovery efforts for student move-out better quantifying the full impact of the reuse efforts. The City would make this software available for other cities to use. A consultant would be hired to manage and report on the grant and would also complete program development and management of the reuse software creation.

In the first year, EC worked with 9 businesses in 4 shopping centers, while in year 2 they worked with 40 businesses in 13 shopping centers. The businesses were a mix of retail, service, and restaurants, each with 1 to over 50 employees. Then they engaged with the employees directly including on-site interviews and training followed by 1 or 2 more visual assessments. \nResults show that in year 1 of the contract, 2 of the 4 shopping centers (50%) had cardboard in their trash, and 2 (50%) had unflattened boxes in their recycling. In year 2 of the contract, 6 of the 13 shopping centers (46%) had cardboard in their trash, 3 (23%) did not have enough capacity for their cardboard, and 9 (69%) had unflattened boxes in their dumpsters. The diversity of businesses engaged by the Ecology Center is representative of the businesses throughout the city, making their data a good reference for our commercial customers overall. To address the issues, the City would hire a consultant to perform the 5 phases of community based social marketing. These are selecting behaviors, uncovering barriers and benefits to the behavior, developing strategies to reduce barriers and amplify benefits, piloting strategies, and implementing broadly with evaluation.

column19: The goal of our LNPK 156 Geothermal Coalition is to analyze and design a 4th generation geothermal district heating system to meet 100 percent of the heating loads of the properties adjacent to the 1.6-mile USDOT RAISE (Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity)-funded rebuild of West Superior Street through LNPK 156. Duluth can be a national example of how innovative design and integration across technologies (transportation, funded by RAISE, and geothermal) can cost effectively accelerate the transition to clean energy and provide communities with resilient heating solutions even in the coldest of climates. The baseline analysis and design will include financial and technical analysis of the use of geothermal heat pumps to recover waste heat from the effluent of the Western Lake Superior Sanitary District (WLSSD) wastewater treatment plant located immediately adjacent to Lincoln Park, as well as development of clear career pathways associated with design, deployment, and operations of the system. Additional analysis will include potential system adds including: 1) Interconnecting the LNPK 156 system and the City of Duluth's district heating system (Duluth Energy System) serving Duluth's Central Business District and the two regional hospitals to further decarbonize the downtown system and provide increased resilience, and financial and environmental sustainability to the broader community, 2) Analysis of incorporating public housing and a community resilience hub into the system (adjacent, but not in the primary footprint), 3) Potential of the system to support snowmelt for the active transportation corridor components and/or newly designed transit stops, and 4) Criteria for expanding support into the adjacent residential area or to assets active in reducing health disparities.

Rencana Penjualan Kredit Karbon dalam Rangka Penutupan Berkelanjutan TPA Terjun Kota Medan

1. Latar Belakang
Seiring meningkatnya timbulan sampah di Kota Medan, kapasitas Tempat Pembuangan Akhir (TPA) Terjun yang telah beroperasi sejak tahun 1993 semakin terbatas dan berpotensi menimbulkan dampak lingkungan berupa emisi gas metana, pencemaran lindi, dan risiko longsoran. Untuk itu, Pemerintah Kota Medan berinisiatif melaksanakan program penutupan TPA secara berkelanjutan dengan mengadopsi teknologi pengelolaan gas metana (landfill gas recovery system) serta memanfaatkan mekanisme perdagangan karbon (carbon credit) sebagai sumber pendanaan alternatif yang ramah lingkungan.
Program ini dilaksanakan melalui kerja sama antara Pemerintah Kota Medan dengan mitra internasional Afvalzorg dan Multriwell (Belanda) serta PT Sumatera Deli Lestari Indah (SDLi) sebagai mitra lokal. Kolaborasi ini menjadi langkah strategis dalam mendukung target nasional pengurangan emisi Gas Rumah Kaca (GRK) dan implementasi kebijakan Net Zero Emission 2060.

2. Tujuan Kegiatan
a) Melaksanakan penutupan berkelanjutan TPA Terjun untuk mengurangi risiko lingkungan dan sosial. 
b) Mengimplementasikan teknologi penangkapan dan pembakaran gas TPA (Landfill Gas Flaring System) guna menurunkan emisi metana.
c) Mendapatkan pendanaan melalui penjualan kredit karbon internasional sesuai dengan persetujuan prinsip Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup dan Kehutanan (KLHK). 
d) Menyediakan lahan TPA yang aman dan dapat dimanfaatkan kembali bagi kepentingan publik.
e) Menjadikan proyek ini sebagai model pengelolaan TPA berkelanjutan berbasis ekonomi hijau di Indonesia.

3. Ruang Lingkup Kegiatan
a) Perluasan area TPA Terjun minimal seluas 4,5 - 6 hektare, membentuk satu badan TPA yang dapat ditutup secara bertahap.
b) Pembangunan sistem pengelolaan gas dan lindi, termasuk instalasi jaringan pipa, flare, dan fasilitas pemantauan.
c) Pelaksanaan studi kelayakan teknis, ekonomi, hukum, dan sosial untuk mendukung pelaksanaan proyek.
d) Pengajuan dan akreditasi kredit karbon melalui lembaga internasional yang diakui pemerintah.
e) Penjualan kredit karbon (CO₂) kepada pembeli potensial dari Korea Selatan, Swiss, dan Belanda.
f) Pelaksanaan penutupan akhir (final capping) dan pemulihan lahan pasca-operasi.

4. Mekanisme Pendanaan
Kegiatan ini tidak menggunakan dana APBD, melainkan didanai melalui hasil penjualan kredit karbon yang dihasilkan dari pengurangan emisi gas metana TPA Terjun (sekitar 392.000 ton CO₂ ekuivalen per tahun). Pendanaan awal dilakukan melalui pra-pembiayaan dari calon pembeli karbon, sedangkan hasil penjualan digunakan untuk membiayai konstruksi sistem penutupan dan pengelolaan gas.
Karena bersifat unsolicited project dan tidak menggunakan dana pemerintah, proyek ini tidak memerlukan proses tender sesuai dengan ketentuan pengadaan kerja sama investasi.

5. Tahapan Pelaksanaan
a) Pra-studi kelayakan (completed).
b) Penandatanganan Letter of Intent (LOI) antara Pemerintah Kota Medan dan Afvalzorg-Multriwell.
c) Persetujuan prinsip penjualan karbon oleh KLHK.
d) Penyusunan studi kelayakan dan penandatanganan MoU kerja sama.
e) Proses akreditasi karbon, penyusunan kontrak, dan pelaksanaan konstruksi penutupan.
Total estimasi waktu pelaksanaan tahap awal hingga MoU adalah 6 bulan, dilanjutkan dengan implementasi proyek sesuai hasil studi kelayakan.

6. Manfaat yang Diharapkan
a) Pengurangan emisi GRK sebesar ±392.000 ton CO₂/tahun.
b) Peningkatan kualitas lingkungan melalui pengendalian gas dan lindi TPA.
c) Optimalisasi lahan untuk fungsi baru yang aman dan produktif.
d) Peningkatan kapasitas kelembagaan dan teknologi hijau di Kota Medan.
e) Dukungan terhadap target pembangunan berkelanjutan (SDGs), khususnya tujuan ke-11 dan ke-13.

Pengolahan Sampah Menjadi Energi Listrik (PSEL) Kota Medan

1. Latar Belakang
Pengolahan Sampah Menjadi Energi Listrik (PSEL) Kota Medan merupakan proyek strategis Pemerintah Kota Medan yang bertujuan untuk mengurangi volume sampah sekaligus menghasilkan energi listrik ramah lingkungan melalui penerapan intervensi teknologi pengelolaan sampah. Proyek ini merupakan tindak lanjut dari Surat Menteri Lingkungan Hidup dan Kehutanan No. B.1307/A/RB.01/10/2025 tentang Intervensi Teknologi Pengelolaan Sampah, serta berlandaskan berbagai regulasi nasional :
- UU No. 18 Tahun 2008 tentang Pengelolaan Sampah,
- Perpres No. 35 Tahun 2018 tentang Percepatan PSEL,
- Perpres No. 109 Tahun 2025 tentang Penanganan Sampah Perkotaan Melalui Energi Terbarukan, dan
- Permen LHK No. P.16/2021 tentang Pengelolaan Sampah.

2. Lokasi dan Karakteristik
PSEL direncanakan berlokasi di TPA Terjun, Kelurahan Terjun, Kecamatan Medan Marelan. Luas area awal yang disiapkan ± 4,98 hektare, untuk pembangunan fasilitas utama, area utilitas, dan zona buffer.
PSEL mengusung konsep Waste to Energy (WtE), yaitu mengubah residu sampah menjadi listrik dengan teknologi ramah lingkungan, antara lain:
- Termal: insinerasi, gasifikasi, atau pirolisis.
- Non-termal: biogas dan RDF (Refuse Derived Fuel).
Kapasitas pengolahan ditargetkan mencapai 1.500 ton sampah per hari, dengan potensi listrik yang dihasilkan sekitar 31-50 MW tergantung efisiensi sistem.

3. Tujuan dan Manfaat Strategis
a) Mengurangi timbulan sampah dan memperpanjang umur TPA.
b) Menghasilkan energi listrik terbarukan dari sumber lokal.
c) Meningkatkan efisiensi pengelolaan sampah perkotaan.
d) Mewujudkan ekonomi sirkular dan menciptakan lapangan kerja hijau.
e) Mendukung target nasional Net Zero Emission 2060.

4. Skema Pembiayaan
Pendanaan dirancang melalui skema campuran (hybrid), yaitu:
- APBN/APBD untuk persiapan lahan dan prasarana dasar.
- KPBU (Kerja Sama Pemerintah dan Badan Usaha) untuk konstruksi dan operasional.
- Investasi swasta dan CSR untuk dukungan tambahan.
- Potensi pendanaan hijau internasional (green finance).

5. Tahapan Pelaksanaan
a) 2025-2026: Pembebasan lahan, studi teknis, dan perizinan. (saat ini sedang dilakukan proses Studi Kelayakan (Feasibility Study) oleh Waste 4 Change).
b) 2026-2027: Pembangunan infrastruktur utama dan instalasi teknologi.
c) 2027-2028: Uji coba operasional, integrasi dengan jaringan PLN.
d) Pasca-2028: Operasi penuh dan replikasi ke wilayah lain.

6. Penutup
Proyek PSEL Kota Medan adalah bentuk nyata komitmen Pemerintah Kota Medan dalam mendukung kebijakan nasional pengelolaan sampah berbasis teknologi dan energi bersih.
PSEL diharapkan menjadi simbol kota hijau dan berketahanan energi, sekaligus mendorong kesejahteraan rakyat melalui lingkungan yang bersih, efisien, dan berkelanjutan.
